{quote}Reject full refund if any partial refund exists.{quote}

Although it is the simplest solution to implement on our side. It’s problematic in the e2e flow for two reasons:

* our refund endpoint is invoked by billing, not by CS - and billing has their own re-try logic, ie. if we fail the full-refund we might end-up in a lengthy loop of retries between billing and us => bad user and CS agent experience, ie. we would need to work with billing and CS how to model this flow that CS understand from the message what and why to do (issue partial refund instead of full)
* Additionally: In APM “overcharge flow” when we charge let’s say 20 EUR from APM, then the actual order is 15 EUR only, we partially refund from payment-core 5 EUR. From PSP point of view there is partial refund already, from CS agent and customer point of view there is not. ie. from “business logic” point of view is the full order refund for 15 EUR OK, but it will fail because of an existing partial refund


Note: on top of that is the full-refund flow slowly being phased out (there is no date, but verticals and their CS flows are in process of switching to the “new refund flow”). The new refund flow works only with partial refund on our end:

I have done a quick bit of research into this issue and IMO our standard position should be to {color:#ff5630}+*not*+{color} email drivers encouraging them to consent to third-party promotions. This is on the basis of the following:

* It strikes me that the key question here is whether such emails would themselves count as ‘direct marketing’ (per the ePD), and therefore require consent in order to be able to send them, or whether we could get away with arguing that they are ‘service messages’ that do not require consent. Admittedly, this is a grey area in EU law / case law (including Cyprus), and there are few sources that directly take a stance on this.
* However, we can assume that such emails are more likely to be considered as marketing messages rather than service messages, given that: (i) the ultimate purpose of these emails is to send more marketing comms to the driver; (ii) in 2017, the ICO fined a few companies for sending emails to users encouraging them to consent to marketing (at the time, the ICO said “_Sending emails to determine whether people want to receive marketing without the right consent, is still marketing and it is against the law_”); and (iii) there are some (limited) secondary sources that take the view that consent would be needed here (e.g., [here|https://dpnetwork.org.uk/email-marketing-rules/]).
* We also would not be able to rely on soft opt-in here, as it would likely fail the ‘similar products or services’ limb.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
In terms of where this leaves us, IMO we should take a *waterfall approach* depending on the riskiness of the jurisdiction / how flexible the stakeholders are willing to be.

* *Plan A*: Advise the business that we should not be sending such emails, as they are likely to require consent themselves. Instead, we should remind drivers to enable consents to third-party comms through less ‘direct' means (e.g., banners, or ‘in-time’ requests for consent where a driver is visiting a specific partner offer on the relevant page).
* *Plan B:* If the business insists on sending these emails and the country is not high risk, we can allow these emails to be sent provide that we ‘de-risk’ them (i.e., make them as administrative / factual as possible, and remove any ‘encouraging’ elements from them).
* *Plan C*: If the business insists on sending these emails and either: (a) the business wants the emails to ‘encourage’ drivers); or (b) the country is ‘high risk’ from a marketing POV, we can advise the business strongly of the risks and that is that.
{panel}

*Q1: Can Bolt bring the add-ons/features to the Finnish market without significant regulatory risks?*

* OC: Yes. The three features (business account payment, ride booker and single invoicing feature are unlikely to significantly increase the current regulatory risk-level.

*Q2: Single invoicing feature: Is there a re-classification risk (as a transportation service) under Finnish law?*

* This feature is unlikely to increase the current regulatory risk-level (i.e. Bolt regarded as a transportation service subject to a Finnish taxi transport license). We note that some of the Finnish taxi dispatch companies (e.g. Taksi Helsinki) provide similar features to their corporate customers in the market. In Finland, the taxi transport license is required from the fleet companies / independent taxi entrepreneurs and therefore, this feature alone is unlikely to increase Bolt’s re-classification risk.

*Q3: Ride booker: are there any specific requirements relating to the Ride Booker under Finnish law?*

* OC: No. Some of the Finnish taxi dispatch companies (e.g. Taksi Helsinki) provide similar features to their corporate customers in the market.

*Q4: B2B contract: are there any mandatory and specific requirements applicable to the add-ons/features under Finnish law?*

* No. There are no local mandatory and specific requirements in relation the referred add-ons/features under Finnish law. Business-to-Business relationships and contract terms are largely governed by the freedom of contract in Finland.

Agreement reviewed on 13 October 2025 and comments provided to [~accountid:6151cf6878e5e40070fb74c2] as follows.

----

*On exclusivity (generally):*

* We should be comfortable on the reclassification side if this setup is acceptable from a competition law perspective.
* The 2-year minimum term in the draft is the absolute maximum I’d consider acceptable. Anything longer should be reduced.
* If they are consulting externals anyway, it’s worth asking for their view on how this is seen in their market.

*On commercial need:*

*  Worth confirming whether exclusivity is actually required on top of the KPIs.

*On pass-down obligations:* we can reduce risk by:

* avoiding obligations imposed on drivers unnecessarily. All obligations should rest with the fleet.
** _Example: Section 11 should not refer to controlling driver behaviour. It should simply prohibit the fleet from using a vehicle for a given purpose._
* avoiding obligations that apply outside the platform.
** _Example: Section 8.3 (“Partner shall ensure that all Drivers hold and maintain all Licences...”) should be limited to when accessing the platform._
* avoiding doubling up on obligations that already ought to be covered by the standard access-to-platform agreement - for example s.8.3 above is already covered in the service provider terms template.
* avoiding KPIs tied to specific individuals. The current setup, where KPIs are tied to vehicles, is good.
* confirming that Bolt does not require specific drivers to use specific vehicles. Ideally, it should be clear that the fleet decides who uses which vehicle.

⚠️ +*Important:*+ Bolt does not reimburse Drivers for losses resulting from counterfeit payments. It is the Driver’s responsibility to verify the authenticity of cash before accepting it, in line with Maltese law.

*Overview & Legal Context in Malta*
In Malta, the use or possession of counterfeit money is illegal. According to the Central Bank of Malta Act (Article 50):

_“(…) a person who is in possession of any counterfeit currency note or coin shall be obliged to withdraw from circulation such currency notes or coins which that person knows or has sufficient reason to believe to be counterfeit, and shall immediately deliver it over to the Bank.”_

The Counterfeit Surveillance Unit monitors and examines seized counterfeit currency in Malta. 
If someone suspects a note is fake, they should notify the police immediately, since using counterfeit money is as illegal as producing it. 

So, if a Rider pays a driver using a fake euro banknote in Malta, that’s a serious offense, and the incident should be reported properly.

Additionally, please note that:

* Attempting to spend or pass on a counterfeit note is itself a criminal offense.
* Counterfeit notes are not eligible for reimbursement by the Central Bank.

*Actions to be taken by Driver*
If a Driver suspects they’ve received counterfeit money:

* Do not spend or destroy the note.
* Contact the Police immediately to report the incident and file a report.
* Surrender the suspected note to the Police or to the Central Bank of Malta as soon as possible.

The Driver can also contact the Counterfeit Surveillance Unit of the Central Bank of Malta:
Phone: +356 2550 6012 or +356 2550 6013 
Via the Bank’s contact form or by mail to the Currency Operations Office, Castille Place, Valletta.

*How to check if a Euro banknote is fake*

Use the “Feel - Look - Tilt” method recommended by the European Central Bank:

*Feel*
Genuine notes have raised print (especially on the words and numbers).
The paper should feel crisp and firm.

*Look*
Hold the note against the light. You should see:

A Watermark
A security thread
A see-through number

*Tilt*
Tilt the note to check the hologram:
The € symbol or number should change appearance.
On the reverse, the colour of the value numeral changes depending on the light.

I found the following information regarding Driver’s licence (shared in this [old ticket|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-31482]):

*Question asked by previous Catarina:* “_Driving license -> We only have a few couriers who use a bicycle which don't need a license however the rest have an engine vehicle so will surely need. In this regard, could you also clarify what would be the risk for Bolt of having couriers active in the platform with expired driving licence and whether we can accept international driving licence?”_

*Response presented by F&F:* 

“_Risk for Bolt of having couriers active in the platform with expired driving licence_ 

_First of all, we understand that all the vehicles used by the couriers are not owned and registered in the name of Bolt (but registered in the name of the Courier or the Delivery Partner). Based on our aforementioned understanding that Bolt does not employ the couriers directly, our initial reaction is that from a transport regulatory standpoint, the fact that Bolt couriers are active on the platform without a valid driving license - should not - in principle give rise to any transport regulatory implications as any responsibility should ultimately fall on the Delivery Partner and/or the Courier directly, and not Bolt itself. However, aside from the transport regulatory aspect, the provision of services by couriers who do not possess a valid driving license could still potentially expose Bolt to legal implications. In the case of a service provided to a consumer, by Bolt (through an unlicensed Courier – I.e. a courier who is not in possession of a driving license) while Bolt would be one step removed from vicarious liability (culpa in eligendo imposed on employers who employ employees who are unfit or uncapable to do the job) we cannot completely exclude the potentially liability of Bolt where there is an issue with the performance of a contract or damage to third parties or third party property. Furthermore, one should also keep in mind any potential reputational damage which may arise from the fact that Bolt may be using couriers who are not in possession of a valid driving license (and who are associated to Bolt as they are giving a service contracted through the Bolt platform, or wearing the Bolt Uniform or “thermobag”) This risk could be mitigated by ensuring that the Delivery Partner is obliged contractually to only employ Couriers who are validly licensed to drive vehicles in Malta and to work and reside in Malta.”_


So, from a *transport regulatory standpoint*, Bolt is not directly exposed if couriers operate without a valid driving licence — liability in such cases rests with the *courier* or *Delivery Partner*, especially since vehicles are not registered to Bolt and couriers are not our employees.

However, legal counsel did flag *residual risk* in two key areas:

* If a customer suffers damage or injury due to an unlicensed courier, Bolt could still face a *claim for poor performance* or *negligent selection*, even if not legally at fault.
* There is a *reputational risk* if it becomes public that an unlicensed courier was active on the platform under the Bolt brand.

Given this, I think it might be worth to raise this topic tomorrow in our “Malta Crisis Response” meeting, where PP and PR can give their contribution.

In any case, should we move forward with this, we can assess the viability of reducing these flagged potential risks by:

# Including this as a Fleet obligation in Fleet Agreements (the Fleet to take legal responsibility for compliance with driving and insurance rules);
# Include this obligation in T&Cs / onboarding flows, with a checkbox or declaration from the partner/courier.

LMK if you agree with this approach. Thank you!

Polina Novikova has identified that there is a data protection / data privacy consideration for this piece of work. 

Please review the ticket and if needed, then please create a sub-ticket for the Privacy team.

What the current Agreements allow:

* Fleet Agreement (Clause 4.2) gives Bolt the right to:
- Hold the fleet responsible for cash collected during deliveries;
- Set off unpaid cash transfer obligations against what Bolt owes the fleet.
* Courier T&Cs (Clause 8.9 & 8.11) cover:
- The obligation of couriers to repay Bolt for outstanding debt;
- The right for Bolt to send data to debt collection agencies.

What is missing:

* There is no clause explicitly stating that courier debt becomes fleet debt.
* No clause authorizes Bolt to deduct courier-related debts from the fleet’s account just because of courier inactivity.

So, even if the intention and commercial logic are clear, in my view the legal basis for automatic deduction (especially if the debt was originally between the courier and Bolt) is currently weak. This means that, jf challenged, a fleet may argue that it is being made liable for a third party’s default without contractual basis — especially if it did not approve the specific courier's onboarding or was unaware of the debt.



Possible recommendation:

* Update fleet contracts to include a clause along the lines of: _“The Fleet shall remain responsible for any negative balances or unpaid cash obligations arising from couriers assigned to its fleet account, regardless of whether such obligations arise during or after a courier’s period of active engagement. Bolt shall have the right to deduct such amounts from any payments due to the Fleet.”_

This clause makes assignment of liability clear and enables legitimate deductions.

Additional measure: notify the fleet of pending debt before deduction;


Next measure:

* Raise it to the global legal team or policy owner for a wider review.

h3. ⚙️ *Recommended Safeguards:*

# *Data minimisation*  
Export *only identifiers necessary for audience matching* (e.g., hashed emails or device IDs).

#* Store the dataset in a *restricted, access-controlled environment* (i.e., only Ads team members who need it can access).

h3. ⚖️ *Good-to-Have / Risk-Mitigation Measures (recommended, not critical)*

#* Although not legally required under _legitimate interest_, consider limiting the audience to users who have *consent enabled to receive direct marketing* (best proxy: those who have *email* marketing enabled for Promotions&Tips).

+*INTERNAL UPDATE (13.10)*+

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*The Law:*
{panel}

We can only collect and store BSN if local Dutch law _specifically_ allows it (Article 46 UAVG) ⚠️ 

* Consent cannot be used as a legal basis here. 
* DAC7 requires Bolt to collect and report tax identification numbers (TIN). *_If BSN needs to be reported to the tax authorities_* in this context, we would have a legal basis for collecting and storing it.
* There do not appear to be any other obvious legal grounds for collecting and storing BSN.

If we were permitted to collect BSNs, we could do so via a (unredacted) copy of the driver’s ID, but we would need to do the following(i) 

* *Remove unnecessary data*: Ideally, we should extract the BSN from the ID copy immediately, store it separately on our systems, and then redact it from the ID copy. This would ensure it is not unintentionally processed for other purposes.
* *Store it only for the specific purpose allowed by law*.
* *Be transparent on precisely why we need this info*.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Feedback from stakeholders*
{panel}

Per discussions [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/D09GKKPKR19/p1758644505421789], [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09HRT9BFDE/p1758734623136559] and [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C05NYVA7T2A/p1755098033151739]:

* BSN would only be the same as / be part of TIN in certain cases, not all cases.
* For fleet drivers (or private drivers operating via a legal entity), we would be providing the driver’s VAT code to the tax authorities. This is different to BSN. As such, we would only theoretically need BSN for private drivers operating as natural persons.
* To get a taxi licence in the Netherlands, private drivers must at least register as a ‘zzp’ (self-employed, without staff). However, BSN does not form any part of the TIN for zzp drivers. Instead, we report the VAT number (BTW-id) of these drivers to the tax authorities, which we specifically request during the signup flow. 
* NB. We also do not collect BSN via any separate flows. It seems we only collect it from the driver card / back of driver licence, list it as the ‘personal code’ on the driver’s profile, and use it for duplication checks. This would be difficult to justify to the regulator.

As such, we do not need to report BSN to the tax authorities → *We do not appear to have a legal basis for collecting and storing BSN* ⚠️ 

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Advice*
{panel}

I provided updated advice to the stakeholder team [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C05NYVA7T2A/p1760370959919529?thread_ts=1755098033.151739&cid=C05NYVA7T2A].

HI [~accountid:5e3d437d9749d00c924cb0f5] Let me explain you 😄 

As I mentioned in the details of this request, it's common for cars to be rented in Paraguay, and as a result, many drivers never remove the vehicles from their profiles. Sometimes, drivers who still have a car registered stop using their accounts and don't request the car's removal. In another scenario, some drivers fraudulently continue to use the registered car even though they no longer physically possess it.

Furthermore, in Paraguay, a car is permitted to be registered to up to 3 accounts. In some cases, drivers who no longer have the vehicle physically maintain a copy of the documents and fraudulently complete a car application process (carapp). This might be because they have cars that do not meet local requirements.

Currently, this process has already been defined in conjunction with the Operations area, which is why we need the process to be "official" and reflected in the KB.

Finally, given the local context in Paraguay, it doesn't make much sense to implement the process of requesting a new car application process . This would mean duplicating the process previously completed by the driver who is the legitimate owner of the car. Additionally, when the request is submitted, it might be rejected if the car exceeds the maximum number of drivers that can have the vehicle registered, as mentioned above

If you need a *report*, please refer to FleetX (DriverX). If your request concerns an *invoice*, follow these steps:

3. Open the driver or fleet profile.
4. Go to the **Invoice tasks** tab.
   * If you see *Invoice sum too small*, no commission invoice was generated because the driver either owed no commission or had more compensation than commission.
   * If you encounter any other error, please let us know.
5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under **Invoice tasks** or **Partner Invoices**.

{quote}Hi Marten,

PayPal follows card network rules (e.g., Visa, Mastercard) and its own internal policies for how long an authorization remains valid:

For most card-based authorizations, PayPal’s system automatically sets the expiration to 29 days.

Within that window, the merchant can capture, void, or reauthorize the transaction.

If no action is taken, PayPal automatically expires the authorization on day 30. I think this has been discussed a while ago. 

This “Authorization Expiration Date” field you see in the PayPal portal simply reflects that maximum validity period in PayPal’s system. It tells you the last day you can capture before the authorization lapses — it does not reflect the actual status of the hold at the buyer’s bank. There is no further change being made, it will not change again. 

If you want to retrieve the “real current status”, you could either use the API call “getTransactions details”. 

A manual approach would be to check the transaction status in the “activity report” in PayPal account. [https://developer.paypal.com/docs/reports/online-reports/|https://developer.paypal.com/docs/reports/online-reports/|smart-link] 

If you require an automated API approach, I suggest to that  ProcesOut and I align to potentially enable them to provide you with the required access. [@salma.taouss@processout.com|mailto:salma.taouss@processout.com]/ [@Roshan Gorasia|mailto:roshan@processout.com] - let me know if you already support GetTransacionDetails API or if there is a possibility to add that to your service (provided it works in your general set-up).

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

* If we are applying a fixed fare, with a compensation being paid by Bolt to the driver to cover the difference between the fare and the taximeter, this is fine, please see the memo [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zy-03gfbK93rEno-497czaGkRpzpPtq6vOfXzxq4q38/edit?tab=t.0].

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The Payments engineers are currently working on sending the right refund amount for these cases where a partial refund was previously made automatically. 
In the meantime, could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The Payments engineers are currently working on sending the right refund amount for these cases where a partial refund was previously made automatically. 
In the meantime, could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

Hey Alon! Some follow up questions:

# If during driver registration we get a relevant biometric consent, then it will be compliant to compare against their photos, correct?
# If yes, then the drivers should be able to withdraw the consent or delete their data, even after they were blocked?

[~accountid:712020:e840ae87-a302-434d-b51c-92daae9cdbce] - to answer your questions from 14 October 👇

✅ *1. Consent during registration*
Yes — if we obtain a _separate, explicit, and carefully worded_ biometric consent during registration (meaning the driver can still register _without_ giving that consent), then we could rely on it for inclusion in the Biometric Database.
Out of curiosity, what’s your current thinking here — would this be presented as part of a “Selfie-Check” (i.e. integrated with a verification step) or as a standalone consent box?

⚖️ *2. Withdrawal and deletion*
Yes, they must be able to withdraw consent. Once consent is withdrawn, we can retain non-biometric data (e.g. account info, incident logs, etc.), but biometric data itself (selfies, facial templates, etc.) must be deleted — since consent is the _only_ valid lawful basis for that processing.

🧠 *3. Blocked drivers (including fraud/safety cases)*
Same principle applies — consent withdrawal rights remain. However, we could retain _other_ data needed to investigate or defend against fraud, safety incidents, or legal claims. What we _cannot_ retain or reuse* is the biometric data itself (unless we can clearly demonstrate a different lawful basis, which in practice is very difficult).

For completeness, as mentioned before, if we isolate and store _embeddings_ separately — ensuring that:

* the embeddings cannot be traced back to identifiable images without special access, and
* only a small, controlled group of engineers can technically re-identify them,

*then the risk of that data being treated as* *_biometric_* *or* *_personal_* *data is reduced (though not eliminated) — this means that the Business could make a risk-based decision to either: generate the embeddings without originally getting consent, or, get consent as you’ve proposed and retain the embeddings and image data after account deletion, on the basis that both are treated as ‘personal data’ and not ‘biometric data’*.

Let me know if that’s clear or if you have further questions.

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] with the correct user ID 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds

{noformat}---------- WAITING STATE -------


SELECT 
round(CAST((x.hour_scheduled-u.order__hours_before_ride) AS double),-2) AS change_in_hours_rounded,
approx_distinct(o.id,0.0041) AS count_order,
approx_distinct(o.user_id,0.0041) AS count_user
FROM ng_public.company_order AS o 
JOIN (SELECT date_diff('hour',cos.created,cos.pickup_time) AS hour_scheduled,
		cos.created,
		cos.pickup_time,
		cos.city_id,
		cos.order_id,
		cos.state
		FROM ng_public.company_order_scheduled cos
		) AS x ON x.order_id = o.id AND x.city_id = o.city_id
JOIN ng_pii.etl_user_order_request u ON o.search_token = u.search_token_id AND u.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -1, current_date) AS date)
WHERE o.payment_method_type <> 'default'
AND o.state = 'waiting'
AND o.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -1, current_date) AS date)
AND o.country = 'ae'
--AND x.hour_scheduled/NULLIF(u.order__hours_before_ride,0) > 1.2
AND x.hour_scheduled-u.order__hours_before_ride > 1
GROUP BY 1
LIMIT 1000{noformat}

As a rule of thumb, we can offer to refund users via Bolt Balance but they have the right to refuse, in which case we should refund to the original payment method or potentially to another payment method of their choice. Goodwill compensations are an exception, as they are not refunds but rather small compensations Bolt choses to issue users in order to minimise their frustration when the service has been provided without any issues.
{panel}

The problem with Bolt Balance refunds is that we cannot take it back afterwards. So, if the user is unsatisfied with the Bolt Balance refund  afterwards, Bolt has to choose either to refund again to the payment method (= double refund) or leave the customer unhappy (= risk of complaints/disputes). Another issue we had was that partial refunds were not possible with Bolt Balance, but perhaps not really relevant here and I believe it has been fixed.

In Portugal we have commission netting.

_Through commission netting, your campaigns/bonuses/compensations are reflected as a discount from your commission, instead of each having their individual invoices. Simply, your commission is reduced in the amount of your campaigns/bonuses/compensations - ensuring a more clear invoicing process, and less invoicing noise._

_For example, previously you would see a commission of 416.91€ and separate bonus lines of 11€ on your invoice, which totaled up to 361.92€. Now, you would only see a single row of commission in the amount of 361.92€, meaning the calculation is already done in the background._

* {{bqs_order_try_id}}
* {{bqs_order_properties}} - order properties as captured by the driver behaviour system
* {{bqs_driver_id}} - admin ID of the driver
* {{bqs_is_force_positive}} - boolean to show whether the driver score signal was force positive
* {{bqs_is_positive}} - boolean to show whether the driver score signal was positive
* {{bqs_negative_rules}}
* {{log_event}} - type of the event (here ‘driver_score_manual_override’)

In terms of the CBCR Transition Safe Harbour and Qualified Financial Statements, most jurisdictions listed in the CBCR report use financial statements that are the accounts used to prepare the consolidated financial statements of the UPE.

There are a few exceptions - UK, UA, and TR - where we rely on statutory financial statements. This approach is justified from a TP perspective. Based on a call with Deloitte on 14 October 2025 this is acceptable as long as it is applied consistently across all entities within the same jurisdiction. In other words, if multiple entities operate in the same country, they must all use the same type of financial statements.

An additional exception is *AZ*, where the tax book is currently used. This is +unlikely+ to qualify as a Qualified Financial Statement, so we will either need to change our approach in the CBCR to use consolidated or statutory FS, or a full GloBE calculation will be required for that entity. We should discuss internally how to approach this case [~accountid:608e5558f0db1300698c69d4] .

Finally, note that entities can change the type of financial statements used (from statutory to consolidated and vice versa) on a year-to-year basis, provided there is a valid justification and the approach remains consistent over time.

Hi [~accountid:712020:de758114-46c6-491b-85be-d23fd9c4b6ad] - I have taken a look at this and my thoughts from a privacy POV are below.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*In short*: The preferred approach would be to {color:#ff5630}+*not*+{color} send emails to drivers encouraging them to consent to third-party marketing. +*Instead*+, we can encourage drivers to enables such consents through less direct/ general means (e.g., in-app banners or a general reminder on the partner offers page).
{panel}

(i) The *rationale* behind this is as follows:

* There is a risk that emails encouraging drivers to consent to third-party marketing could _themselves_ be regarded as direct marketing, which we cannot send to to drivers unless we have obtained their consent (some regulators have explicitly said that sending these kinds of emails without consent is “_unlawful_”). This would undermine the core purpose of sending the email in the first place. As such, we can only encourage drivers to enable these consents where such encouragement would not qualify as ‘direct marketing’.
* The easiest way to do this would be to ensure that the encouragement is not ‘+direct+’ (i.e., not targeted at specific drivers, such as via emails, push notifications, SMS texts etc.). Non-targeted ways of encouraging drivers would include in-app banners and general reminders on the partner offers page. It strikes me that this would have the same end result, and so would be a sensible approach.
* Alternatively, we could try and take steps to stop the emails from being ‘+marketing+’ (i.e., making them administrative / neutral in tone, rather than encouraging), however this is not recommended from a privacy POV as it is risky (i.e., regulators may still find that such emails are marketing and fine Bolt if we have not collected the driver’s consent already).

Happy to discuss if you have any questions on this 🙂

* Partners need to have registration with Bulgarian Food Safety Authority, so please check that new partner has appropriate registration. To check it you need to do the following:
** Go to: [https://public-iisr.bfsa.bg/|https://public-iisr.bfsa.bg/|smart-link] 
** Select: Национален регистър на обектите за производство и дистрибуция на храни и материали и предмет, предназначени за контакт с храни и странични животински продукти (National register of facilities for the production and distribution of food and materials and objects intended for contact with food and animal by-products); 
** Then select specific registries depending on type of business activity of the partner:
*** For restaurants: Регистър на обекти за обществено хранене (Register of public catering establishments)– this includes restaurants, fast food establishments, bistros, diners, coffee shops, etc.
*** In case they were not in restaurant’s list, please check list for grocery stores just in case: Регистър на обекти за търговия на дребно (Register of retаil establishments)– this includes supermarkets, stores selling food supplements, other packaged food stores
** Then input the relevant Registration No. provided by the Partner to confirm their registration

* In Bulgaria we need to send to the authorities list of Partners that we work with every time there are changes regarding who our Partners are. I will discuss the solution with Dimitar on how to efficiently collect information.

{code:sql}%sql
    SELECT *,

           GREATEST(gmv_price_diff - COALESCE(voucher_price, 0), 0) AS total_discounts /* discount (without vouchers) */
    FROM (
        SELECT 
            user_id,
            order_id,
            order_created,
            order_created_local_date, /* <- shows when trip took place */
            ac.country_code,
            is_voucher,
            country.name AS country,
            ebpom.city_id,
            ac.name AS city,
            ebpom.tracking_country,
            gmv_eur,
            gmv_eur_without_service_fee,
            service_fee,
            price_eur_without_service_fee,
            price_currency,
            total_fee_sum,
            targeted_bonus,
            voucher_price AS old_voucher_price,
            ebpom.category_group,
            --ROUND(voucher_price / rate, 4) AS voucher_price,
            --voucher_price AS not_rounded_voucher_price,
            --country2.currency AS tracking_currency,
            --rate,
            -- NEW: correct voucher conversion (company’s home city currency)
            ROUND(voucher_price / currency.rate, 4) AS voucher_price,
            voucher_price AS not_rounded_voucher_price,
            CASE
                WHEN (gmv_eur_without_service_fee - price_eur_without_service_fee) < 0 THEN -(gmv_eur_without_service_fee - price_eur_without_service_fee)
                ELSE 0
            END AS extra_charge, /* additional charges (e.g. price customization), so shows what client paid on top */
            CASE
                WHEN (gmv_eur_without_service_fee - price_eur_without_service_fee) >= 0 THEN (gmv_eur_without_service_fee - price_eur_without_service_fee)
                ELSE 0
            END AS gmv_price_diff, /* >0, diff between what client paid and price -> gmv_price_diff - voucher_price = total_discounts */
            (service_fee + total_fee_sum) AS bb_total_fee_sum, /* includes service fee of BB */
            CASE
                WHEN is_portal THEN 'Business Account'
                WHEN is_wp THEN 'Work Profile'
                ELSE NULL
            END AS payment_profile,
            CASE
                WHEN ebpom.product = 'team account - new portal'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'team account - old portal'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'work profile'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'ridebooker - cash'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'cash ridebooker - API'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'ridebooker - team account'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'ridebooker - old portal'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'team account - API'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'team account - voucher'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'business delivery'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'ridebooker - delivery' THEN 'Rides'
                WHEN ebpom.product = 'rental - business'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'rental - wp' THEN 'Rentals'
                WHEN ebpom.product = 'carsharing - business'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'carsharing - wp'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'carsharing - long term rental' THEN 'Carsharing'
                WHEN ebpom.product = 'business food' THEN 'Food'
            END AS vertical
        FROM ng_public_spark.etl_business_product_order_metrics AS ebpom
        LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_city AS ac 
               ON ebpom.city_id = ac.id /* to get country select * from ng_public_spark.admin_system_city */
        LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_country AS country 
               ON country.code = ac.country_code
        --LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_country AS country2 
        --       ON country2.code = ebpom.tracking_country /* extra join to get tracking currency */
        LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.etl_business_business_company AS business_business_company 
               ON ebpom.entity_id = business_business_company.id
        -- NEW: Use company_country (not tracking_country) for exchange rate
        LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_country AS company_country 
            ON company_country.code = business_business_company.country_code
        LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.currency_exchange_rates AS currency 
            ON company_country.currency = currency.currency
            AND ebpom.order_created_local_date = currency.valid_on

        WHERE order_created >= CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE) and order_id = 2081247395
          AND order_created_local_date >= CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE) /* partition key; shows actual date when trip happened (think scheduled) */
          AND finished_orders = 1
          AND (
              NOT (business_business_company.is_bolt_company)
              OR (business_business_company.is_bolt_company) IS NULL
          ) /* Bolt TA orders are excluded */
    )
    WHERE vertical = 'Rides'
      AND payment_profile IN ('Work Profile', 'Business Account'){code}

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

I already reviewed the contract and made a few suggestions directly in the document. You can find it [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Fm2iFS32Yld7akR0KxAlhuygq0lWGQFP/edit].

In summary:

* Since it won’t be Maxim Milashenko, but Marketa Hlavacova, who will sign the contract, Marketa’s data must be inserted instead;
* On the first clause (“landlords' legitimacy”) I left a comment calling your attention to the fact that the landlord is not the owner of the property, but rather holds the status of usufruct holder (“usufrutuário”). This has legal implications — if the usufruct ends (e.g., by death or any other cause defined in the title), the lease agreement automatically terminates, regardless of any remaining contractual term. Also, I think you should ask for the permanent certificate of the property so we can check the accuracy of it’s description and also the terms of the usufruct.
* Clause 5 - I made small amendments to make it more precise in some aspects (added that the Landord must communicate, in writing and at least 30 days in advance, the adjustment coefficient and the resulting new rent; and specified that payments should be made to the bank account specified in the contract or other bank account indicated by writing by the landlord).
* Clauses 7 and 8 are the ones who suffered the most important changes. The new wording is intended to anticipate and address our main concerns: works and termination.
* In clause 7:
- In point 1, I added that the Landlord wont have any right to demand the removal or alteration of the adaptation works made by Bolt at the end of the contract or to demand any compensation related to or arising from such removal.
- I added a new point 2 concerning the AC: 
_“2 - A Arrendatária poderá instalar, no locado, unidades de ar condicionado (AC) e respetivos equipamentos e sistemas auxiliares (incluindo condutas, motores e suportes), desde que o faça em conformidade com as normas legais e regulamentares aplicáveis, bem como com o regulamento do condomínio, caso exista, responsabilizando-se por eventuais pedidos de autorização junto da administração do edifício, se necessários._
_3 - Sem prejuízo do disposto na Cláusula 7.1, os equipamentos de ar condicionado instalados pela Arrendatária poderão ser removidos no termo do contrato, desde que tal remoção seja possível sem implicar a realização de obras ou alterações estruturais no locado.”_
* In clause 8:
- I made the necessary amendments in point 3 to predict that, during the first five years, we may terminate the contract at any time, provided that we give 240 days' notice; and added a new point 5 predicting that, during the 2 year renewal periods, a 120 days' notice will suffice. As I wrote in our slack channel, I think a 240 days notice is a bit too heavy on us, but ultimately this is a business decision.
- I added a new point 4 predicting that we can end the contract at any time, without any penalty of indemnity, if the installation of the AC is not authorized by the competent entities (namely the condominium administration or public authority), within 60 (sixty) days of signing this contract, as this is an essential condition for the Lessee to carry out its activity, which the Landlords acknowledge.
- In the last number I added that the visits must be previously agreed between the parties.
* In clause 9 - I have slightly amended point 1 to cover not only deterioration resulting from normal wear and tear of the property, but also deterioration resulting from normal wear and tear appropriate to the purposes for which the property was leased.
*  Clause 12 - Changed it having in consideration that it will be Marketa Hlavacova who will sign the contract, and not Maxim Milashenko, and that neither of them can declare that they visited the property (they can only declared that someone from Bolt’s team visited it).
* Clause 13 - I think it is advisable to remove the possibility of communications being done by email. Particularly in our case, this could lead to communications not being seen, which could be detrimental to us. It is better to maintain that communications are valid if sent by registered letter to our head office address, so that we can always be sure that if anything arises in relation to this contract, it will always have to be by that means (for example, we never know when someone designated as the person who will receive communications by email may eventually leave the company, and this, in the worst case scenario, could be highly detrimental to us, because we have an email address specified in the contract that could simply be deactivated).

Please LMK if you have any doubts and, in the meantime, it would be really useful to obtain the permanent certificate of the property.
Thank you!

What was discussed and agreed during today’s (14.10.2025) meeting between Rainer & Liisa regarding showcasing Google reviews of restaurants under DineOut.

# *COMPLIANT PROCESS*

[@liisa.puu|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U05LKNHAZGA] will give final green light tomorrow after discussing it with IP counsel. However, by default we should be ok to proceed with following approach.

# *Obtain or identify the Place ID for each restaurant*

# Use the Places API (e.g. Text Search / Nearby Search) or Autocomplete API to search for the restaurant by name/address. The API returns the Place ID. [Google for Developers+2Google for Developers+2|https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/op-overview?utm_source=chatgpt.com]
# (Optionally) use a “Place ID Finder” UI during onboarding or setup (e.g., input address → get back place ID) to help map restaurants to valid Place IDs. [Google for Developers|https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/examples/places-placeid-finder?utm_source=chatgpt.com]

# *Store the Place ID (only the ID, not the full data)*

# It is permissible to store the Place ID itself (IDs are exempt from the strict caching rules that apply to content). [Google for Developers+1|https://developers.google.cn/maps/documentation/places/web-service/place-id?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com]
# But you should not store or cache the Google-provided content (e.g. rating, reviews) beyond ephemeral or transient display purposes.

# *At runtime, request place details using Place Details API*

# For each restaurant listing in the Bolt Food app, Bolt issues a _Place Details_ request with the Place ID and asks for specific fields (rating, user reviews, etc.). [Google for Developers+2Google for Developers+2|https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/place-details?utm_source=chatgpt.com]
# Use a *field mask* to limit the response to only the needed fields, which helps control costs and avoid unnecessary data retrieval. [Google for Developers+1|https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/usage-and-billing?utm_source=chatgpt.com]
# The API returns a JSON object that includes rating, review count, and (optionally) individual reviews and other metadata. [Google for Developers+2Google for Developers+2|https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/reference/rest/v1/places?utm_source=chatgpt.com]

# *Display the rating (and possibly reviews) in Bolt’s UI, with attribution*

# When showing the Google rating (and possibly reviews) in Bolt’s interface, Bolt must *include the Google attribution* (logo, “Google Maps” text) and cannot obscure or remove it. [Google for Developers|https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/policies?utm_source=chatgpt.com]
# Visually, Bolt should distinguish Google-sourced content from its own content (e.g. via borders, spacing, or shading). [Google for Developers|https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/policies?utm_source=chatgpt.com]
# Bolt must clearly notify users that Google Maps content is used and governed by Google’s Maps terms and privacy policy (in Bolt’s terms or in-app notices) as required by the Maps Platform Terms.

# *Refresh or revalidate Place IDs over time*

# Because Place IDs may change, Bolt should periodically (e.g. once per year or upon failure) refresh the Place ID by making a minimal Place Details request to retrieve the current ID. [Google for Developers+1|https://developers.google.cn/maps/documentation/places/web-service/place-id?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com]
# If a Place ID becomes invalid or the business is removed/closed, the API returns an error (e.g. NOT_FOUND). Bolt must handle those gracefully.

* 4.2 - this clause was deleted. It’s a must have as it makes Customer cover damage/costs from User’s use or legal breaches. I added that it’s applicable only when Business payment method is used, with Bolt to provide evidence on request. (Ideal version in AZ language exists)
* 7.2 - liability cap tied to amounts paid during the entire agreement term. Way too open-ended exposure, especially if it’s a multi-year deal.
* 7.3 - they’ve left only one liability carve-out (when Huawei gives us incorrect data), so with the current drafting we’re exposed for almost everything else - including driver/provider performance, platform outages, and data loss - i.e., risks we don’t control.
* Our GTC 6.4 - removed. Just like with 4.2, this creates a gap where Bolt lacks a clear contract basis to recover fees or costs arising from usage under Huawei’s Business account (incl. unauthorised/fraudulent use). This leads to higher dispute/chargeback risk, bad-debt exposure, and “moral hazard” (Customer controls access but can deny responsibility).
* 7.5 - they added daily penalty on total agreement value for delays or unresolved “poor quality.”
This converts Bolt into direct service provider with open-ended financial exposure. I cannot approve this as we’re an intermediary, not a transport operator.
* 7.8 - they added that Bolt is responsible for service quality, Customer can self-remedy or hire third party and Bolt pays resulting damage. Same as with previous point: I cannot approve this as we’re an intermediary, not a transport operator.
* 10.6 - they’ve added a non-payment/offset right on termination for Bolt breach. If Customer terminates, they say nothing outstanding is payable, they can claim amounts from Bolt, and they only pay for “flawlessly performed” services. Why this is a problem: We’re an intermediary with post-payment billing - rides are already consumed when invoiced. This language lets them withhold payment for services already used, turn any minor issue into “not flawless,” and offset/claim broadly, creating bad-debt risk and ongoing disputes.
* 11.2 - they’ve added that any amendments/annexes only by mutual written consent. This means that we cannot change our GTCs without their consent and this can be a big problem in case we need to change something urgently due to regulatory changes, or we want to improve the product and need to reflect that in the terms, etc. This is an essential right for us.
* 11.6 - no assignment rights unless written approval has been received (this includes intra-group  assignments)

* <> Legally, I can’t sign off on these changes. Given how long negotiations have continued without movement on the key points, further back-and-forth is unlikely to get us to signature. I suggest you to make a business call now: either proceed with the risks or step away.

Higher iROI targets however, make the expanded error shrink

* Explain what’s the assumption behind different uncertainty for different spends
At lower spend, the uncertainty is lower. This is defined by the shape of the selected curve we’re having signups = vmax*cost/(vmax+cost)
Technically, this curve is our own selection (we could have selected any other).
But the selection is guided by the fact that we believe that there should be no curves that saturate immediately (i.e. we assume curves should saturate gradually)
So if we have two curves (e.g. the true one vs the measured one), the difference between predicted signups will go to 0 as spend decreases, will go to vmax1-vmax2 as spend increases.

* Why we do not want to use just the average wMAE across all channels for now (going for share of ”certain” budget instead).
** It’s because it is the metric that makes least sense (especially when aggregated)
** wMAE is neither business-interpretable, nor representative about the error (while the share of “certain“ spend is at least interpretable)
* Why we might not want to show option 3 (the cost interval scenario):
** It seems to be the option that is misunderstood by the stakeholders. Once they see it, they immediately think of it as of scenarios.

Potential Question from stakeholders:

* Markets with higher GMV should be more robust for business. Why are we saying they are less certain?
** This is because the impact is more robust in terms of general outputs (i.e. getting a user in Germany gives you 180 GMV in a year)
** But when it comes to getting to an accurate GMV, it actually does not help us (+-180 GMV). 

Question: 

* Why are the intervals also assymetric? E.g. in NL we were showing [0.6;2;7]
** Answer is: it’s due to actual vmax being very low and us having to trim the variance.
** E.g: actual vmax = 10, sd = 100, so vmax should be in the region [-90, 110]. But at the same time, it cannot be -90, so had to trim to 0.

Under  GDPR, the Fleet Owner (FO) does *not* have an independent right to access CCTV footage if Bolt is the *data controller* for that footage. The key legal basis lies in *Articles 4, 6, and 15 of the GDPR*, along with supporting recitals and national data protection interpretations (by the Danish Data Protection Agency, _Datatilsynet_). Here’s how it breaks down:

----

h3. ⚖️ *1. Controller vs. Processor (§4(7) GDPR)*

Under *Article 4(7) GDPR*, a _data controller_ is the entity that “determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data.”
If Bolt controls when, how, and why CCTV footage is recorded and used — for example, for safety, loss prevention, or incident review — then *Bolt is the data controller*, not the Fleet Owner.

The Fleet Owner may act as:

* A *processor* (if processing on Bolt’s behalf), or
* A *separate controller* for different purposes — but *not* for footage controlled by Bolt.

👉 Therefore, the FO cannot claim a direct right of access to data that Bolt controls.

----

h3. 🔐 *2. Lawful Basis for Sharing (§6 GDPR)*

Under *Article 6(1) GDPR*, processing (including disclosure) is lawful only if one of the listed conditions applies, such as:

* (c) legal obligation
* (f) legitimate interest
* (a) consent
* (e) public interest / exercise of official authority

In this case:

* There’s *no legal obligation* (no police report or authority request).
* There’s *no legitimate interest* sufficient to override Bolt’s or data subjects’ privacy rights.
* There’s *no consent* from the individuals filmed.

👉 Without one of these bases, *Bolt cannot lawfully disclose the footage*.

----

h3. 👁️ *3. Right of Access (§15 GDPR)*

Under *Article 15 GDPR*, the _right of access_ applies only to *data subjects themselves*, not to third parties or Fleet Owners.
Even the data subject’s right is subject to limitations — for example, when disclosure would adversely affect the rights of others (*Article 15(4)*).

👉 A Fleet Owner asking “on behalf of” someone else or for their own operational reasons does *not qualify* as a data subject request.

----

h3. 🧾 *4. National Practice (Denmark)*

The *Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet)* has confirmed that:

* CCTV recordings fall under the responsibility of the _data controller_ (the operator determining the purpose and use).
* Disclosure to third parties is only permissible under a *clear legal basis*, such as a *police request* or *explicit consent*.

See Datatilsynet guidance on _TV-overvågning (CCTV)_:

{quote}"Optagelser må kun videregives, hvis der er hjemmel hertil – fx til politiet i forbindelse med efterforskning af lovovertrædelser."{quote}

(Source: [http://Datatilsynet.dk|http://Datatilsynet.dk|smart-link]  – TV-overvågning)

*On the question of who currently has (or should have) access to the footage - controllership over the personal data:*

* The FO does *not* have access to the CCTV himself (in most other markets, the FO would usually be considered controller, and Bolt would have no access or control whatsoever over the filmed content) - I assume this is the case here, as he would otherwise not be coming to you to request the footage.
* In contrast, Bolt *should* have the requested CCTV content in DK - but this is unfortunately not the case at the moment due to the difficulties encountered in securing a provider.
➡️ From my own GPT research, I found the following:
In Denmark, taxi operators are legally required to have CCTV installed in vehicles under the Executive Order on Taxi Services (Bekendtgørelse om taxikørsel). However:
* The controller of the CCTV footage is normally the company or entity that operates the taxi permit (the licence holder).
* Fleet Owners (FOs) can sometimes be the controller _if they own and operate_ the vehicles _and_ the CCTV system is installed under their licence and for their drivers.
* If, however, the cameras are part of a centrally managed or integrated system (as is the case for Bolt, where the data would be processed via Bolt’s technical environment), then Bolt or the Bolt entity in Denmark would remain the data controller for that processing.
➡️ In short:
* If the CCTV is part of Bolt’s system/infrastructure, Bolt is the controller. The FO does not have independent access rights.
* If the FO independently installed the camera and operates it under their taxi permit, then the FO could be controller (and must ensure compliance with Danish CCTV law, including signage, retention, access controls, and registration with the Danish DPA if applicable).
➡️ Given your note that _“we currently don’t have a CCTV setup since the integration broke after the acquisition”_, this strongly suggests that:
* The cameras are (or were) Bolt-controlled, not FO-controlled.
* Therefore, FOs should not have access to the footage, and disclosure to them would be unlawful unless a formal authority request is received.
So, in this DK setup, Bolt Operations OÜ (and/or its Danish entity) remains the data controller for any CCTV data related to rides provided via the Bolt platform.

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] with the correct user ID 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt or previous failed payment that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Gemini’s response 
Based on my analysis of the free-text cancellation reasons from the spreadsheet, here is a proposal for the top 10 cancellation reasons for riders in Abuja, followed by a selection of the top 5 with justifications.

h3. Top 10 Proposed Cancellation Reasons:

# *Driver asked me to cancel:* This was a very common complaint, indicating that drivers are frequently requesting cancellations, which can be frustrating for riders.
# *Driver was unprofessional or rude:* Many riders reported negative interactions with drivers, including rude behavior, unprofessionalism, and arguments.
# *Driver was going in the wrong direction/took too long to arrive:* Riders frequently cancelled due to drivers not heading towards the pickup location or having excessively long ETAs.
# *Driver's vehicle did not match the app description:* This includes discrepancies in the car model, license plate, or color, which can be a safety concern for riders.
# *I could not contact the driver:* Riders reported being unable to reach the driver through the app or by phone.
# *Driver refused to go to my destination:* Some drivers would refuse the trip after seeing the destination, often citing reasons like traffic or distance.
# *I found a better/cheaper ride:* This indicates that riders are price-sensitive and will switch to a competitor if they find a better offer.
# *My plans changed/I no longer need a ride:* This is a rider-centric reason that is important to include for accurate data.
# *I was not ready for the ride:* This covers situations where the rider needs more time before they are ready to be picked up.
# *Safety concerns:* This is a broad but crucial category for capturing any situation where the rider felt unsafe.

h3. Top 5 Recommended Cancellation Reasons and Justification:

From the list above, here are the top 5 reasons I recommend for inclusion in the app, with a justification for each:

# *Driver asked me to cancel:*
#* *Reasoning:* This is the most critical issue to track. It directly points to a driver behavior that negatively impacts the rider experience and can manipulate the system. By making this a primary option, you can gather data on which drivers are frequently exhibiting this behavior and take appropriate action.
# *Driver was unprofessional or rude:*
#* *Reasoning:* The quality of the driver is a key factor in rider satisfaction. This reason allows you to identify and address issues with specific drivers, which can help improve the overall quality of your service and rider retention.
# *Driver was going in the wrong direction/took too long to arrive:*
#* *Reasoning:* This addresses a core functional aspect of the service. Long wait times and inefficient routes are major friction points for riders. Tracking this helps identify potential issues with your mapping and dispatching system, as well as drivers who may be inefficient.
# *Driver's vehicle did not match the app description:*
#* *Reasoning:* This is a significant safety and trust issue. Riders need to be confident that they are getting into the correct vehicle. By tracking this, you can identify fraudulent or non-compliant drivers and take immediate action to maintain the safety and integrity of your platform.

Hi [~accountid:5cefbeb5b457f80f23adba60] ! I am getting back to respond to your question about the *Bolt’s ability to reuse user data when moving to its own payment services from Airwallex* ⤵️ 

h2. *Summary*

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
Under our agreement with Airwallex, *Bolt’s ability to reuse user data when moving to its own payment services is partially limited.*

The limitation only applies to *data that was collected by Bolt solely on behalf of Airwallex for Airwallex’s own compliance and onboarding purposes*, specifically:

* *Onboarding Data* gathered under Airwallex’s KYC and AML requirements;
* *Additional Verification Data* requested by Airwallex compliance;
* *Support Data* where Bolt handled user support for Airwallex products.

All other data that Bolt collected and controlled for its own platform operations remains *fully usable* for transitioning users to Bolt’s native payments solution (i.e. user account data, payout data, etc.).
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*To understand the impact, I suggest the following next step:*

* Map the data fields needed for Bolt’s new payment onboarding;
* This will allow privacy team to understand which portions of that data fall within Airwallex’s exclusive control and we could update our agreement before the EU launch to fix this.

 It is also important to note that users’ existing *direct relationship with Airwallex will continue* even after Bolt discontinues Airwallex integrations - Airwallex will remain an independent controller for its own customers.
{panel}

----

h2. 

*Detailed Explanation*

h3. *Overall Structure of the Data Sharing Agreement with Airwallex*
The DSA creates two key data-sharing models between Bolt and Airwallex:
* *Controller-to-Controller (Module 1):* Each party processes its own users’ data for its own business purposes.
* *Processor-to-Controller (Module 4):* Bolt processes data strictly on Airwallex’s instructions, acting as Airwallex’s data processor.
Only the latter category introduces reuse restrictions.
----
h3. *2. Data Bolt Can Freely Reuse*
When Bolt acted as a *data controller* (Module 1), it collected and processed:
* Partner, rider, and delivery user data (including contact, account, and payout information).
* Any onboarding or support data gathered for Bolt’s own operational purposes.
This data is *Customer-Controlled Data*.
Bolt can continue to use it independently, including for:
* Transitioning users from Airwallex products to Bolt’s native payment services; and
* Operating and improving those payment services.
There are *no contractual restrictions* in the DSA preventing such reuse.
----
h3. *3. Data Bolt Cannot Reuse*
When Bolt acted as a *data processor* (Module 4), it collected data purely on Airwallex’s behalf, including:
* *Onboarding Data* gathered under Airwallex’s KYC and AML requirements;
* *Additional Verification Data* requested by Airwallex compliance;
* *Support Data* where Bolt handled user support for Airwallex products.
This information is *Airwallex-Controlled Data*.
Contractually, Bolt:
* May process it *only as instructed by Airwallex*;
* *Cannot combine or reuse* it for its own purposes (e.g., onboarding users to Bolt’s own financial products);
* Must *delete or return* it when the Airwallex integration ends;
* Cannot retain copies for Bolt’s new services without Airwallex’s separate consent.
Therefore, any data that was collected *solely for Airwallex’s onboarding and compliance* cannot be repurposed for Bolt’s new payments license activities.
----
h3. *4. Continuing Relationship Between Users and Airwallex*
Users who opened Airwallex accounts as part of Bolt’s embedded finance integration remain *direct customers of Airwallex*.
When Bolt discontinues Airwallex’s services on its platform, these users’ *Airwallex accounts will continue independently*, governed by Airwallex’s own privacy and contractual terms.
Bolt’s new payment products will constitute a *separate service relationship*, and any data Bolt wishes to use for onboarding those users must come from Bolt-controlled sources or new collection.

What do we need to do in order to process all volumes through CheckOut? 

* Move card verification to CheckOut. — The biggest blocker here is MADA cards need a special requirement. Mada does require *3ds + cvv.*
* Move Mada co-scheme payments to CheckOut 
MADA cards need a special requirement. Mada does require *3ds + cvv* for the first time where you add the card and get the src_id (permanent token of the card). After that if you want to pay with a saved MADA, you can process it without 3ds + cvv, by processing it as MIT (merchant initiated transaction):
--> merchant_initiated: true,
--> previous_payment_id: pay_id (the payment ID where you saved this card)
--> source.stored: true
--> source.store_for_future_use: false
--> payment_type: Unscheduled or Recurring (based on the type)
[https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C010VCJ4T3Q/p1760093423877359?thread_ts=1756202066.399299&cid=C010VCJ4T3Q|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C010VCJ4T3Q/p1760093423877359?thread_ts=1756202066.399299&cid=C010VCJ4T3Q|smart-link] 
* Move Mada ApplePay Payments to CheckOut — *source.store_for_future_use*: is set via a feature flag at the gateway level — meaning that in order to have it *false* for apple pay and *true* for normal mada debit cards, you would need two gateways on PO with the same cko credentials. 
This might interfere with ApplePay MIT Mada payments if the details are not stored for future use. 
MIT payments are not supported for Mada ApplePay
* Improve the fallback rate. — The payment analytics team has done an analysis on payments that have a high success rate when they fall back to Adyen. Clarifying with CheckOut if there is anything we can do to improve CheckOut SAR error messages [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02HE1GDHTQ/p1760428983064169|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02HE1GDHTQ/p1760428983064169|smart-link] 
* AMEX cards are not being accepted via CheckOut. - Haitham needs to sign the agreement with CheckOut.

* -Create a new connection for CKO with the same credentials-
* -Ask PO to configure the new connection with the MADA ApplePay requirements-
* How to disable MIT payments for MADA ApplePay - Disable overcaptures? 
* Haitham the CKO account owner needs to enable Mada card on CKO portal
* Ask the local team for help with MADA cards testing. 
* Test card adding with MADA 
* Test card payment with MADA
* Test applepay payment with MADA

Based on our research, it appears that private operators can lawfully engage in regular waste collection in Malta, provided they are registered as waste carriers with the Environment & Resources Authority (ERA) and comply with all applicable permit conditions and local council requirements. However, the ability to operate in a given locality will depend on whether there are existing exclusive municipal contracts in place, and whether local councils require coordination or prior approval for private waste collection activities.

While we understand the comparison made with Bolt Send, it’s important to note that waste collection is legally distinct from passenger or goods transport and is subject to its own regulatory and licensing framework. We will need to liaise with the relevant authorities to confirm whether the proposed model can operate lawfully under current rules.

*Key regulatory considerations:*

* Under the Waste Regulations, any entity acting as a waste carrier or broker must be registered with the ERA.
* We also need to determine whether the delivery of waste to disposal or processing sites must be pre-authorised or accepted by the relevant waste treatment operators.

*Points to note:*

* Vehicles used in this service must be individually registered as a waste carrier with ERA.
* The type of waste being collected matters — different categories (e.g. municipal, bulky, hazardous) may require additional permits or compliance obligations.
* Noncompliance (e.g. using unregistered vehicles, improper handling, or transporting unauthorised waste) may result in fines, denial of access to disposal sites, or regulatory action.
* Some municipalities have exclusive contracts for waste collection — offering competing services in those areas may trigger contractual or legal risks.
* Any incident during transport (e.g. spillage, improper storage) could expose the fleet operator — and potentially Bolt — to environmental liability or reputational harm.

*To proceed with a full assessment, we first need to clarify the following:*

# Where will the collected waste be delivered?
Which facilities or disposal sites will the service rely on?
# Do you already have — or expect to secure — fleet partners who are registered (or willing to register) as licensed waste carriers with ERA?

Given the above, we’d like to reconfirm whether this is indeed the model you are aiming to pursue, and whether the necessary supply side (compliant fleets) is realistically in place.

After your confirmation, we are happy to proceed with a detailed legal review of the applicable framework. Please allow us a couple of weeks to complete this assessment, as it envolves a lot of regulations and matters.

Thank you!

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.

h2. WBR specific mart

I think this makes sense, but this is not such a high priority. What I tried to do [here|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/dashboards/27659] with WBR backfill monitor was pretty much that. 

If ops gave us the exact list of metrics or let us see where their starting point is where they take it over and do their spreadsheet thing afterwards, we could build something more specialized for WBR and mb we don’t even need to optimize existing pipelines, but make a separate one sort of for WBR only and if it runs way quicker, just because it runs a lot less stuff it seems to me to be a good way to achieve that goal so that it loads before 4am or however early it was that they wanted it

I would be against though creating models on top of stg, unless they are in exact same folder and labeled as ad hoc, because if they are accidentally reused by somebody this would create dependencies that are really hard to resolve

*TLDR:* I think it might be a good idea, if we can do it without modifying our current setup too much and just creating something use-case based for WBR, otherwise imo it might turn into something huge

h2. Broader picture

I’m not sure what would be the better place to note it down, but it seems that this topic will be closely related to marts/etc. I had an idea about our general setup

h3. Suggestions

h4. Extend data modelling layer definitions and lock some layers down

*Layers to lock down. Created by AEs, extra formulas can be added by analysts, but created and configured(incremental, etc.) by AEs*

* Staging. Cleaning up sources

This stays as is, but needs to be polished and approached with scale. E.g. data tests, automations, etc.



* Intermediate > Facts. Pure event logs, without joins + relevant single table based formulas. E.g. timezone casting
* Intermediate > Dims. Object snapshots without joins + relevant single table based formulas. E.g. extra categories like age of a user from date of birth
* Intermediate > Derived(Denormalized). Combinations of facts and dims that are very often used together. E.g. dim_city and dim_country, dim_region can be left joined to create dim_place. Similar with facts(usually relevant for funnels) e.g. order_try to order

The point of this is to have building blocks for analytic entities



* Entity(new). Joins of various facts and dims and derived.

Manual joins. What we currently do very often in fact tables and as a result it gets overlooked. The idea is to create tables with the widest possible reusability so that we try to narrow down SoTs as much as possible and for every table the lineage exploration upstream of this is always 4 steps



* Semantic. on top of entity 1:1 to entity, Metrics as they are, except based on higher number of entities that are already pre-joined. Metricflow doesn’t do any joins. That way the parse tree will be much smaller and mf faster. But very strongly support metricflow. Really cool stuff 🙂 



* Marts
** Universal. What we currently try to do with marts on different grains, but with revised approach. We integrate metrics, backfills are built-in into the logic by default. 
*** Metric flow explains are saved. We use dbt union_relations and stuff like this + scripting
** Ad-hoc. Fully up to analysts they can do whatever in there and due to that we don’t have any ownership and we also do not provide support on the ad-hoc marts
