Hi [~accountid:712020:1d5390cd-af56-43c8-9d12-f431b20183ba], I’ve reviewed the Collaboration Agreement. Below is a *summary of the key commercial provisions* to be aware of. *Please still read the full agreement so you’re familiar with all obligations on Bolt.*

I’ve also marked up the attached agreement with *proposed amendments* we might negotiate initially — please see a summary of my amends below.

h1. 📄 *Summary of the Collaboration Agreement*

----

h2. ⚙️ *General*

* The agreement starts on signing and continues until *8 October 2026*, extendable by mutual agreement at least 60 days pre-expiry.
* Bolt must cooperate with the council on Projects which need to be formalised via a *Schedule 1 template* — either party can propose a Project and it only becomes operative once signed by both parties.

----

h2. 💰 *Charges and Payment — Clauses 8–10 and Schedule 1, Part 3, Clause 5*

* No charges unless a Project Schedule says otherwise; if it does, invoices per that schedule; 30-day payment terms; no set-off (except tax). Interest at BoE base +4% (floor 4%).
* *£275 per permitted bike per annum*, calculated against the fleet cap (e.g., 700 cap = £224,583 for the 14-month period to 8 Oct 2026, ex-VAT).
* Exceedance charge also £275/bike/year based on average daily exceedance per six-month period.
* Payment options: lump sum (30 days before signing), 12 monthly or 4 quarterly instalments; exceedance fees due within 30 days.
* Early Council-initiated termination triggers pro-rata refund of pre-paid charges.
* Fees are regulatory cost-recovery, not consideration for services; Council may withhold/suspend deployment if fees are 30+ days overdue.

----

h2. 🔐 *Data Protection — Clause 12 and Schedule 1, Part 3, Clause 4.7*

* Please ensure that the privacy team reviews these clauses.

----

h2. 🛡️ *Indemnity — Clause 17*

* Bolt indemnifies the Council for third-party IPR claims related to tech/data and for operation/use/parking/condition/maintenance of bikes — this has a cap of *£10,000,000*.

----

h2. 🧾 *Insurance — Clause 18*

* Please ensure that this clause is reviewed by @Daniel Severin. 

----

h2. ⚖️ *Limitation of Liability — Clause 19*

* Standard carve-outs (death/injury, fraud, title) plus {color:#ff5630}*breach of confidentiality (11), data privacy (12), and IPR (13) are outside the cap*{color}.
* Where insurance is required under clause 8, liability is limited to that insurance level; otherwise *£10,000,000*.

----

h2. ⏳ *Termination — Clauses 20–21*

* Project Schedules can be terminated by either party on 3 months’ notice or for material breach. Severance leaves the rest of the Agreement intact.
* The agreement may be terminated for non-payment (30+ days after notice), material/repeated breach (30-day cure), insolvency events, change of control, warranties untrue, and force majeure. Either party may terminate on 6 months’ notice. 
* The Council may also terminate or vary on 30 days’ notice if law/policy changes or a new regulatory/licensing scheme is introduced.

----

h2. 🏙️ *Commercial Background — Schedule 1, Part 3, Clause 2*

* Westminster operates a mandatory bay-parking model for e-bikes/e-scooters.
* Approx. 5,955 spaces at 392 locations (219 marked + 173 virtual), of which 4,682 for dockless bikes and 1,273 for e-scooters.
* Limited, temporary virtual bays at under-utilised cycle stands may be used (50% shared use) until more physical bays are provided; no deployment in cycle stands/virtual bays (ride must start/end in designated bays).
* The arrangement is *not a concession*; no exclusive rights; the Council acts solely in its regulatory capacity.

----

h2. 📍 *Geofencing and In-App Mapping — Schedule 1, Part 3, Clause 2.3*

* Whole borough is a No-Parking Zone except designated bays; polygons must match Appendix map and be updated within 48 hours of changes.
* Users cannot end trips outside bays; minimise GPS buffer to 0m.
* Provide real-time API access (e.g., Bluesystems), submit parking compliance and end-of-ride photos, and monthly KPIs.

----

h2. 🛠️ *Permission and Operations — Schedule 1, Part 3, Clauses 2.4–2.5*

* Bolt’s licence may be withdrawn for safety/capacity/legal reasons.
* Bolt must publish Bolt contact details on all vehicles.
* There will be a monthly ops group with the Council.
* There will be no recompense where bays are suspended for works/events—operators must adjust fleet.

----

h2. 🚲 *Service Management (Core Operational Obligations) — Schedule 1, Part 3, Clause 4*

[~accountid:712020:1d5390cd-af56-43c8-9d12-f431b20183ba]*, please ensure you and our Ops teams review this section in full.*

* *Parking & removal SLAs:* Entire borough is no-parking except bays; users can’t end outside bays. Removal timings: non-danger/non-obstruction best endeavours 2h, max 4h; obstruction immediate and within 1h; emergencies—Council/Police may remove. Repeated failures lead to warnings; {color:#ff5630}*3 in 1 month = licence revoked.*{color}
* *Fleet cap & redistribution:* Initial max 700 bikes (increase only with Council approval). Performance criteria for increases include utilisation (guidance 4–6 trips/day), availability (90%), and parking compliance (90%+). Maintain balanced distribution; comply with Priority Areas (0630–1900); restore compliance within 24h; 48h notice for zone changes. Auto-deactivate power in No-Riding Zones with in-app explanation.
* *Maintenance:* Keep bikes roadworthy/charged/clean; service centre records; spot-check after battery swaps, proactive inspections, battery strategy.
* *Removal SLAs:* minor tech/cleanliness etc. 24h; obstruction ≤4h; danger ≤1h; emergencies - Council/Police may remove; Bolt bears removal/storage costs if Council acts.
* *Customer service & education:* 24/7 contact channels; in-app training covering where to ride, zone rules, safe riding, and how to park (incl. disability awareness); app must show real-time parking locations.
* *User penalties:* at least £10 from the second parking offence; escalating measures for repeat/high-risk behaviours.
* *Safety & enforcement:* Notify serious incidents within 1 hour; cooperate on enforcement; maintain banned-user records; take responsibility for theft/vandalism/abandoned bikes.

----

h2. 📊 *Reporting — Schedule 2*

[~accountid:712020:1d5390cd-af56-43c8-9d12-f431b20183ba]*, please ensure you review this section in full.*

* Monthly safety/utilisation and quarterly ESG/education metrics to be provided free of charge for the term.

----

h2. 📚 *Council Policies — Schedule 3*

* These have been referenced in the agreement but not provided so *we’d need to request these from the council*.

----

h1. ✏️ *Changes I Have Provisionally Made and Suggest We Negotiate*

----

* *Indemnity - Clause 17:* narrowed the indemnity by (i) excluding indirect/consequential loss and loss of profit, and (ii) adding a carve-out so the indemnity does not apply if the Council is negligent or at fault. I retained the £10,000,000 cap.
* *Limitation of liability - Clause 19:* revised the general cap to the lower of £10,000,000 and the insurance actually maintained for the relevant risk.
* *Termination - Clause 21.4:* included that the council must give 60 days’ notice to vary/terminate for changes in law/policy or a new scheme and where a change materially increases Bolt’s costs or reduces capacity, Bolt may terminate on 30 days with a pro-rata refund.
* *Geofencing & mapping Schedule 1, Part 3, clause 2.3:* increase the location tolerance to a 1m buffer (rather than a 0m buffer).
* Increased the deadline for Bolt to resolve any failure to comply with the service management principles following receipt of notice from 48 hours to 72 hours.
* *Parking & removal SLAs – reset the SLA ladder:*
** Non-danger/obstruction: best endeavours within 3h; absolute max 5h;
** Danger/obstruction: immediate and ≤2h;
** Defined “receipt of notification” as 06:00–22:00, with out-of-hours deemed at 06:00 next day;
** Added that council removal costs must be reasonable and evidenced.
* *Warnings / loss of permission:* increased the threshold that 5 (was previously 3) written warnings within one month may lead to revocation and fleet removal.
* Lowered the utilisation criteria to increase the total fleet from 4–5 trips per day, per vehicle to 1–3 — this should give Bolt more flexibility to increase the total fleet.
* Lowered the availability and parking compliance criteria from 90% to 80% — again, allows Bolt more flexibility to increase the total fleet.
* *Schedule 1, Part 3, clause 4.3(b):* amended so that Bolt must use “reasonable endeavours” to achieve the 06:00 daily 50% deployment target, and allowed 48 hours (rather than 24 hours) to correct local exceedances with temporary exceedance now permitted during redistribution.
* *Customer sanctions:* replaced fixed penalties with proportionate, escalating sanctions (warnings/education → temporary block/fines/ban), at Bolt’s discretion, for behaviours like ending rides in no-parking zones or double riding.
* *Schedule 1, Part 3, clause 4.6:* increased the deadline for Bolt to notify the Council of a serious incident from 1 hour to 2 hours.
* *Charges:* included that nothing in the agreement restricts Bolt from charging users under our customer terms.
* Removed *section 3 (Confidential Information)* from Schedule 1 as I believe this contradicts clause 11.1(a) of the main agreement.

h3. *Summary*

Assess the feasibility and implications of running the *Failed Order Optimisation (FOO)* test in Denmark, considering the country’s competitive landscape and price-regulation framework. The outcome should determine whether current conditions support testing or if adjustments or safeguards are required prior to rollout.

----

h3. *Background*

Szymon proposed a 4-week, user-based FOO test that offers riders an optional price increase when an active order is likely to fail, then restarts matching at the updated price. The feature has produced measurable uplifts in completion rate and GMV in several markets; however, Denmark’s competitive and regulatory context differs substantially and requires closer evaluation before implementation.

----

h3. *Objective*

To conduct a comprehensive evaluation of FOO’s compatibility with the Danish market, addressing potential risks, competitive positioning, and regulatory compliance — particularly regarding dynamic pricing and fare ceilings.

----

h3. *Key Considerations*

* *Market competition:* Uber currently outperforms Bolt in Denmark on both pricing and ETA. Any feature that may result in higher rider prices — even on a voluntary basis — could affect conversion and user perception in an already price-sensitive market.

*Denmark – Decision on Failed Order Optimisation (FOO) Test*

*Date:* 16 October 2025
*Prepared by:* Pema Matos 

----

h2. *Overview*

Following an internal review, Denmark has decided *not to proceed* with testing the _Failed Order Optimisation (FOO)_ feature at this time.
The decision is based on market competitiveness, pricing regulations, and the potential impact on rider perception.

----

h2. *Background*

The FOO feature identifies trips likely to fail and offers riders the option to increase the price voluntarily to improve matching success. The initiative has produced positive results in some international markets.
However, Denmark’s market conditions and regulatory framework differ significantly, requiring a more cautious approach.

----

h2. *Key Considerations*

h3. *1. Competitive Landscape*

* The Danish market is currently *highly competitive*, with *Uber outperforming Bolt* on both *price* and *ETA*.
* Any feature that could lead to higher visible prices, even voluntarily, risks reducing *conversion* and *price competitiveness*.
* Maintaining stable, predictable fares is essential to preserve rider trust and market share.

h3. *2. Price Regulation*

* Denmark operates under *national price regulation*, which caps allowable fare levels.
* The combination of *FOO and surge pricing* could, in certain scenarios, push fares above the *regulatory ceiling*.
* Implementing such a feature without full legal and technical safeguards poses *compliance and reputational risks*.

h3. *3. Consumer Sensitivity*

* Danish riders are *price-conscious* and compare platforms before booking.
* Sudden or unclear price changes often lead to *lower satisfaction*, *complaints*, and *reduced loyalty*.
* Current consumer sentiment favors *transparency and fairness* in pricing.

----

h2. *Decision*

Denmark will *not test the FOO feature* at this stage.
The focus will remain on improving pricing consistency, ETA performance, and operational efficiency before revisiting optional price adjustment mechanisms.

Check using correct dashboard profit calc:

*Looker dashboard code (order_id: 2184840500)*

{code:sql}%sql
    SELECT *,
           (bb_total_fee_sum /* + extra_charge */ - ((gmv_price_diff - COALESCE(voucher_price, 0)))) AS profit, /* Bolt earnings - rider incentive (Bolt cost (vouchers are not cost)) */
           GREATEST(gmv_price_diff - COALESCE(voucher_price, 0), 0) AS total_discounts /* discount (without vouchers) */
    FROM (
        SELECT
            user_id,
            order_id,
            order_created,
            order_created_local_date, /* <- shows when trip took place */
            ac.country_code,
            is_voucher,
            country.name AS country,
            ebpom.city_id,
            ac.name AS city,
            ebpom.tracking_country,
            gmv_eur,
            gmv_eur_without_service_fee,
            service_fee,
            price_eur_without_service_fee,
            price_currency,
            total_fee_sum,
            targeted_bonus,
            voucher_price AS old_voucher_price,
            ebpom.category_group,
            --ROUND(voucher_price / rate, 4) AS voucher_price,
            --voucher_price AS not_rounded_voucher_price,
            --country2.currency AS tracking_currency,
            --rate,
            -- NEW: correct voucher conversion (company’s home city currency)
            ROUND(voucher_price / currency.rate, 4) AS voucher_price,
            voucher_price AS not_rounded_voucher_price,
            CASE
                WHEN (gmv_eur_without_service_fee - price_eur_without_service_fee) < 0 THEN -(gmv_eur_without_service_fee - price_eur_without_service_fee)
                ELSE 0
            END AS extra_charge, /* additional charges (e.g. price customization), so shows what client paid on top */
            CASE
                WHEN (gmv_eur_without_service_fee - price_eur_without_service_fee) >= 0 THEN (gmv_eur_without_service_fee - price_eur_without_service_fee)
                ELSE 0
            END AS gmv_price_diff, /* >0, diff between what client paid and price -> gmv_price_diff - voucher_price = total_discounts */
            (service_fee + total_fee_sum) AS bb_total_fee_sum, /* includes service fee of BB */
            CASE
                WHEN is_portal THEN 'Business Account'
                WHEN is_wp THEN 'Work Profile'
                ELSE NULL
            END AS payment_profile,
            CASE
                WHEN ebpom.product = 'team account - new portal'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'team account - old portal'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'work profile'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'ridebooker - cash'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'cash ridebooker - API'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'ridebooker - team account'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'ridebooker - old portal'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'team account - API'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'team account - voucher'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'business delivery'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'ridebooker - delivery' THEN 'Rides'
                WHEN ebpom.product = 'rental - business'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'rental - wp' THEN 'Rentals'
                WHEN ebpom.product = 'carsharing - business'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'carsharing - wp'
                  OR ebpom.product = 'carsharing - long term rental' THEN 'Carsharing'
                WHEN ebpom.product = 'business food' THEN 'Food'
            END AS vertical
        FROM ng_public_spark.etl_business_product_order_metrics AS ebpom
        LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_city AS ac
               ON ebpom.city_id = ac.id /* to get country select * from ng_public_spark.admin_system_city */
        LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_country AS country
               ON country.code = ac.country_code
        -- OLD: exchange rate was based on ebpom.tracking_country (sales team’s country) - incorrect for voucher currency
        -- LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_country AS country2
        --       ON country2.code = ebpom.tracking_country /* extra join to get tracking currency */
        LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.etl_business_business_company AS business_business_company
               ON ebpom.entity_id = business_business_company.id
        -- NEW: now based on business_business_company.country_code (company’s registered/admin country)
        -- LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_country AS company_country
        --    ON company_country.code = business_business_company.country_code
        -- NEW2: now based on city_id -> country_code -> exchange rate
        LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_city AS company_city
          ON company_city.id = business_business_company.city_id
        LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_country AS company_country
          ON company_country.code = company_city.country_code
        -- Exchange rate
        LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.currency_exchange_rates AS currency
            ON company_country.currency = currency.currency
            AND ebpom.order_created_local_date = currency.valid_on

        WHERE order_created >= CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE)
          AND order_created_local_date >= CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE) /* partition key; shows actual date when trip happened (think scheduled) */
          AND finished_orders = 1
          and order_id in (2183587732, 1438908775, 2184840500)
          AND (
              NOT (business_business_company.is_bolt_company)
              OR (business_business_company.is_bolt_company) IS NULL
          ) /* Bolt TA orders are excluded */
    )
    WHERE vertical = 'Rides'
      AND payment_profile IN ('Work Profile', 'Business Account'){code}

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

# Termination - The City may revoke or terminate the License “*at any time for any reason*” at the Manager’s sole discretion - which means they could terminate it for any reason at all, even without a breach on our side. If it is a curable violation we would have 30 days. If it is non-curable we would have a 90 day removal period. No compensation for sunk costs. I would like to suggest amending this clause so that it builds in a 30-day notice for convenience termination but there is no way to do that without changing the entire clause quite a bit. hey [~accountid:63998438f3c3dfd71fe85ae4]  — this bug is partially valid. I can reproduce it, but only after the {{Retry OTP}} screen has been shown once before tapping *Resend code* again. Updated repro steps:

# Open the app.
# Log in.
# Continue with phone number.
# Enter a valid phone number and continue.
# The *Enter code* screen appears (fires {{Enter Phone Number Screen Opened}} → {{screen_name = "Enter Code"}}).
# Wait for the *Resend code* button to become active.
# Tap *Resend code* → {{Resend Code Tapped}} fires with {{screen_name = "Enter Code"}} ✔️.
# The *Retry OTP* modal appears ({{Retry OTP Screen Shown}} updates {{screen_name = "Retry OTP"}}).
# Close the *Retry OTP* screen.
# Tap *Resend code* again → {{Resend Code Tapped}} now carries {{screen_name = "Retry OTP"}} ❌.

Same behaviour occurs in the legacy login flow.

h2. Why it happens

On iOS we derive {{screen_name}} from the most recent event of type {{.showScreen}} / {{.changeScreen}}. In the first pass, the last “opened” event is the *Enter code* screen, so the tap is tracked correctly. After the modal is shown, the last “opened” event becomes *Retry OTP*, and closing that modal does *not* emit another “opened” event for *Enter code*. 

Driver presentation logic doesn’t trigger a screen-open event when returning from a modal, the tracker keeps pointing to *Retry OTP*. This is the root cause, and it predates the redesign — nothing in the redesign changed this behaviour.

Hi [~accountid:603cb85ec58c720071175949] , there are two ways (or two steps) how we can handle it:

* *Acknowledge the insurer (without sharing any personal data)*
** Reply to the insurer:
*** Explain that Bolt cannot disclose driver contact details.
*** Say we can relay the insurer’s contact information to the driver so the driver may contact them directly if they wish.
*** Ask them to confirm the single point of contact (email preferred) and reference to quote.
** Do *not* copy the driver or reveal any driver identifiers.

*Suggested response*

{quote}Dear Ms Nouri,

Thank you for your message regarding the incident on 8 October 2025 involving Ms C.S. Margaret.

Please note that Bolt does not hold the registration number of the third-party vehicle involved in this incident. This information was exchanged directly between the drivers at the scene. As drivers are independent service providers, Bolt does not posses the information requested.

In line with our data protection obligations, we are unable to share our driver’s personal contact details with third parties. However, if you wish, we can relay your contact information and case reference to the driver, so they may contact you directly should they choose to do so.

To proceed, please confirm:

* The preferred single point of contact (email address is preferred), and
* The reference you would like the driver to quote in any correspondence.

Once confirmed, we will pass this information to the driver. Please note that it will be at the driver’s discretion whether to respond.

Kind regards,{quote}

* *Reach out to the driver (in-app or email)*

Use the template:

{quote}We received a request from Maya Letselschade B.V. regarding incident 8 Oct 2025 involving your Bolt trip. They are seeking the third-party lorry registration number. If you’re willing, you can contact them directly at [info@mayaletselschade.nl|mailto:info@mayaletselschade.nl], ref MA2025073.
This is entirely optional. If you prefer not to engage, no action is required.{quote}

* *Handle driver responses*
** *Driver agrees:* Ask them to contact the insurer *directly*; do not forward driver details.
** *Driver asks Bolt to share their details instead:*
*** Only proceed if they give clear, written consent specifying what (email vs phone), to whom (insurer details), and why.
*** Prefer sharing an email address over a phone number. Log the consent (store a copy here).
** *Driver declines or no response within 7 days:* Close out with the insurer.
* *Close the loop with the insurer*
** If the driver agreed to contact them: “_We relayed your contact details to our driver. Any follow-up will come directly from them.”_
** If the driver declined or didn’t respond: _“We relayed your request to the driver. They have chosen not to engage / did not respond. Bolt cannot assist further and does not hold the requested registration number. You may wish to obtain it via the police accident report.”_
* *Record-keeping*
** Store (in this ticket): insurer request, our acknowledgement, the driver notice, any driver response/consent (if given), and the final insurer reply.

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] with the correct user ID 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt or previous failed payment that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Afiba

Hi Lucca,

Thanks for sharing this idea. It’s definitely creative and I can see the commercial rationale in trying to reduce licence costs as a barrier to entry.

From a legal and reclassification perspective though, the structure you’ve outlined carries material risk. The way it’s framed (where the loan is written off if the driver completes a certain volume of trips with Bolt) looks less like financing and more like a conditional incentive tied directly to work.

That creates three key concerns:

* *Worker status:* linking debt forgiveness to a threshold of Bolt trips could be viewed as remuneration or a work-related benefit. This undermines the independent contractor model and strengthens dependency arguments.
* *Financial Regulatory Actovity:* a loan or deferred payment scheme could fall within FCA consumer credit regulation, particularly if Bolt funds or promotes it.
* *Tax:* HMRC or the Tribunal could see the loan write-off as taxable income rather than a simple subsidy, with resulting compliance and reporting implications.

We could explore potential alternative ideas that are lower risk if structured correct. For example, partnering with an authorised finance provider or exploring policy-level licensing support with TfL.

*_Tax analysis - Delivery services and License agreement new version review_*

1) +Contracting parties -+ ✅

*Licensor:* KFC Europe Sàrl, Lausanne - Switzerland, CH (“KFC Europe”)
*Licensee:* Bolt Operations OÜ, Tallinn - Estonia, EE (“Bolt EE”)
*Nature of transaction:* Right to use KFC trademarks and related IP in connection with delivery operations under a licensing arrangement (Art. 2 and Art. 4 of the Agreement)

2) +Royalty (Tax pov) -+ ✅

*Definition:* Art. 4.1 of the agreement defines it as _“A monthly license fee payable by Licensee to Licensor, calculated as 6% of any and all revenues Licensee collects and retains from customer orders (including delivery fees and/or any service fees collected by Licensee), plus taxes if applicable.”_
*Substance:* Payment which represents consideration for the use of IP (KFC trademarks and brand assets), and 2) not linked to service provision, but to the right to use IP in commerce. Thus qualifies as royalty for tax purposes under both OECD MC art. 12, and EE & CH domestic definitions.

+3) Withholding Tax (“WHT”) -+ ✅

*Tax law framework:* CH not a EU Member-State, thus EU Interest&Royalties directive (2003/49/EC) does not apply. Therefore, WHT implications should be analyzed under EE domestic tax law, and double tax treaty between CH-EE (“DTT CH-EE”).
a) Domestic EE rule: Under § 29 of the Estonian Income Tax act, royalties paid to non-residents are subject to 10% WHT, unless reduced under a treaty.
b) DTT CH-EE: Under art. 12 (royalties), Estonia may tax royalties arising in EE and paid to a CH resident, but the tax shall not exceed 5% of the gross amount, provided that the CH recipient (KFC Europe) is the beneficial owner of the royalties, and a CH tax residency certificate is provided to EE Tax Authorities.
c) Resulting WHT rate: Default (no treaty proof) at 10%, +Treaty rate (with certificate) at 5%.+ 
d) Other: Bolt to collect and provide a CH tax residency certificate from KFC Europe to EE Tax Authorities. Likewise, Bolt should provide to KFC Europe a WHT certificate to allow the latter for a CH tax credit or exemption on the withheld amount.

*Gross-up clause:* The phrase at the end of of art. 4.1 of the agreement “…_plus taxes if applicable.”,_ does not impose a gross-up obligation; There is no wording such as “without deduction or withholding” or “net of tax”. Thus it refers only to indirect taxes. Therefore, Bolt EE bears the WHT cost and pays KFC Europe the net amount after deduction.

*Example calculation:* See table below

||Item||Amount (€)||Notes||
|Retained revenue|100,000|Total Bolt EE income from KFC deliveries|
|Royalty (6%)|6,000|Base under Art. 4.1|
|WHT @ 5% (treaty)|300|Withheld by Bolt EE and remitted to Estonian Tax Authority|
|*Net payable to KFC Europe*|*5,700*|Bolt transfers this amount|
|*Effective total cost to Bolt EE*|*6,000*|WHT is Bolt’s tax liability, not a gross-up|


+4) VAT+ - ✅

*Place of supply:* Under EU VAT Directive, art. 44 sets that the place of supply for B2B services (inc. IP licensing) is where the customer is established. Thus, EE.
*Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM):* KFC should not charge CH VAT on the invoice. Bolt EE should self-assess EE VAT under RCM rules (Bolt declares and simultaneously deducts the VAT in its EE VAT return, making it VAT neutral).

+5) TP -+ ❓

5.1 - 6% royalty should be at arm´s length with licensing benchmark. (As per what I read, typically 4-8% of net sales). 
5.2 - Do we need to request to KFC (or obtain ourselves) any TP documentation to support the rate and its deductibility?
5.3 - The agreement is meant to cover KFC-Bolt globally (confirmed that not affecting though African markets and AZ). What about those other markets (i.e. RO, BG, UA) where Food business is carried out locally by Bolt LEs? In my view, there should be extra agreements/annexes for those Bolt LEs to engage with KFC Europe, so that the LEs pay the royalty.

would you please clarify whether you see any issues with this Business proposal? 
From my perspective, the solution seems in line with previous assessment shared by DLA in GR. Indeed, according to the GreeK expansion Memo, it is possible for Bolt to apply a *Platform Fee* charged to passengers, *as long as this fee is clearly presented as a separate fee for the use of the Bolt platform/app and not part of the transportation fare*.

Key points:

* The *expansion memo confirms* that Bolt can also apply a *“Platform Fee”* (sometimes called “booking fee”) charged to passengers directly for the use of the Bolt app, provided:
** The fee is *linked to the digital intermediation service* (not the transport service).
** The fee is *clearly disclosed in the passenger terms and app interface* before booking.
** VAT at *24%* applies to the Platform Fee (Bolt invoices it directly to the passenger).
* DLA clarified that *Bolt may collect the Platform Fee*, keep part of it (e.g. in this case €0.65), and *pass the rest (€5)* to the driver, provided payment flows comply with the *PSD2 rules* (i.e. collection by a licensed payment processor or within Bolt’s agent exemption).
* There are *no caps or specific restrictions* under Greek law on the Platform Fee itself, as long as it is not presented as part of the regulated taxi fare (which must follow the taximeter and fare ceilings).

Therefore, the proposed model (passenger charged +€5.65, €5 rebated to the driver, €0.65 retained by Bolt) seems *legally feasible*, assuming:

* It applies *only to in-app rides*, where payment is processed electronically via Bolt.
* The *taximeter fare remains untouched* (the €5.65 must appear separately on the passenger invoice as “Platform Fee”).
* The *fee structure and driver benefit* are *clearly explained in the driver and passenger communications* to avoid confusion or claims of hidden charges.
T&Cs reflect this.

Can you please confirm this is fine also for your point of view?
thank you!
Elisabetta

Thank you for raising the ticket.

You can structure this in a few ways, but the simplest option would be to ignore their PHO licence and have them sign up as a standard fleet.

*CO LEGAL REVIEW*

+*General Points to Flag*+ 

# +Drafting and Structural Issues+ 

* The agreement contains a number of drafting errors / clause numbering errors (e.g. clause 3.2 “_The parties shall collaborate in relation to the Schedule 1s agreed in accordance with 5 (Proposals and Projects)”_ which should state _“The parties shall collaborate in relation to the Schedule agreed in accordance with clause 5 (Proposals and Projects)”_ and clause 15 which incorrectly cross- refers to clauses 16 and 17.
* The agreement includes some drafting notes/square brackets that will need to be tidied up prior to signing (e.g. clause 1.18). 
* Defined terms are not consistent (i.e. “Council”, “Authority”, “Local Authority”) and need to be tidied up. 

# +Structure of the agreement+ 

There is *no risk here, however it’s worth flagging for your information*. The agreement is not a traditional commercial contract - it is a collaboration framework that sits above specific operational projects.

* The collaboration agreement (i.e. the ‘framework’) sets the general legal and commercial relationship between Bolt and the Council. It does not itself authorise deployment of e-bikes - the Project Schedule does. 
* Each Project Schedule (e.g. as set out in Schedule 1, Project Schedule – Dockless Bikes) governs a specific project. If we were to enter into separate projects with the Council, they would be entered into by way of Project Schedules that ‘plug into’ the overarching collaboration agreement.  
* Please review Schedule 1 - Dockless Bikes carefully as it sets out all core commercial and operational obligations (fleet caps, parking rules, removal SLAs, KPI reporting and data requirements).

# +Term, duration and termination+ 

* *Commencement:* (i) the agreement begins on the date both parties sign (clause 2.1) and (ii) the Project Schedule begins on an agreed “Commencement Date” (Schedule 1 clause 3)
* *Duration:* the agreement and Project Schedule continues until *8 October 2026, after which it expires automatically* (clause 2.2). 
* *Extension:* (i) the agreement can be extended by mutual written agreement, but must be signed at least 60 days before expiry (clause 2.3), and (ii) the Project Schedule can be extended simply by mutual agreement in writing (Schedule 1 clause 3). 
* *Termination rights:*
** Either party can terminate for convenience on *six months’ notice (clause 21.3).*
** The *Council may terminate* or vary with *30 days’ notice if any law, policy or regulation changes, or if a new licensing regime* is introduced (clause 21.4). *NOTE:* we recommend deleting this clause as we risk having our operations terminated at short notice due to any changes in policy/regulations. 
** For cause: Either party can terminate for material breach (with a 30-day cure period) or insolvency (clause 21).
** *Project-level:* Either party can terminate an individual Project Schedule with *three months’ notice or for breach* (clause 20.3).

+*Key Risks*+ 

# *Financial & Revenue* 

* *Fixed annual charge and exceedance fee (Schedule 1 clause 2 “Charges”)*

_Risk:_ *Bolt must pay the Council £275 per permitted bike per year*. The same rate also applies to any average daily exceedance above that cap, calculated over each six-month period. The Council also has the right to withhold/suspend Bolt’s right to deploy bikes if any charges or exceedance fees remain unpaid for more than 30 days.

_Impact:_ this structure fixes our cost base regardless of how the service performs (i.e. we would still be paying for bikes that may not have many RPV during the Winter season, for example). *Note that* our maximum fleet size on day one will be *700 bikes* and we cannot exceed this without explicit permission from the Council (Schedule 1 clause 4.2.7). 

_Suggestion:_ (i) consider what fleet cap is most appropriate for Bolt,  (ii) agree the fleet cap with Westminster accordingly and (iii) ensure that the agreed fleet cap is clearly reflected in Project Schedule to avoid any dispute/inconsistency. 

# *Liability & Insurance* 

* *Broad indemnity in favour of the Council (clause 17)* 

_Risk:_ Bolt indemnifies the Council for all third-party claims connected to the bikes or service, *“whether or not the Council has been negligent or at fault.”*

_Impact:_ This goes beyond a normal fault-based indemnity. We could be liable for accidents caused by the Council’s own street layout, defective signage, or bay design. The indemnity also covers consequential loss (profit, reputation) and defence costs on a “full indemnity basis”, creating effectively unlimited exposure.

_Suggestion:_ ideally we would delete the indemnity in its entirety. However, if this is not possible, the next best option would be to (i) delete the phrase “whether or not the Council has been negligent”, (ii) exclude indirect or consequential losses from the indemnity to keep exposure insurable and (iii) limit the maximum aggregate liability under the indemnity to either a much lower sum that’s reflective of the contract value or 100% of the total charges paid by Bolt under the Project Schedule. If the Council pushes back, we recommend aligning the aggregate cap to £5 million to mirror the insurance cover (see below) and ensure that confidentiality, data and IP liabilities are included within the cap.  

* *Unclear liability cap (clauses 18 - 20)*

_Risk:_ public liability and employer’s liability cover is required at £5 million (clause 18) but the liability cap in the limitation clause is £10 million (clause 19.6) and some heads of losses (e.g. confidentiality, data, IP) appear uncapped because of drafting errors/inconsistencies. 

_Impact:_ this disconnect means we risk having twice the exposure our insurance actually covers, and potentially unlimited liability for data or IP breaches. 

_Suggestion:_ as with the indemnity, amend the liability cap to a much lower sum that’s reflective of the contract value or 100% of the total charges paid by Bolt under the Project Schedule. If the Council pushes back, we recommend aligning the aggregate cap to £5 million to mirror the insurance cover and ensure that confidentiality, data and IP liabilities are included within the cap. 

# *Operational* 

*Please read through Schedule 1 carefully as these contain commercial/operational details. Note in particular the following operational points which may be onerous:* 

* *Clause 4.2:* 
** We must introduce no-parking zones and ensure that rides cannot be successfully ended within such zones or outside designated parking locations. 
** We must remove non-compliant bikes within *1 hour* (if parked in a way that causes a danger or obstruction) or *4 hours* (if parked outside agreed parking locations but not causing danger or obstruction). 
** Failure to remove a bike within the timeframes may lead to removal by the Council/Police and we will be liable for the cost of removal and storage. 
** If we receive three written warnings within a one-month period, the Council will revoke our permission to operate and remove our bikes from the area. 
* *Clause 4.3:* 
** We must always have a minimum of 50% of the permitted maximum fleet deployed in each operational zone at the beginning of each day (0600 hours). 
** The Council may amend operational zones, priority areas, or no-riding areas with 48 hours’ notice. 
* *Clause 4.4*
** Maintenance regimes of the bikes must include spot checking after every battery change, regular and pro-active inspection for wear and tear, a strategy and process for maintaining and recycling of electric batteries. 
** Note the timescales for repair/removal of bikes under clause 4.4(e) and check that these are acceptable in practice. 
* *Clause 4.5*
** Note that we are required to enforce penalties on riders who engage in high-risk behaviour and non-compliant parking - such penalties must be set at a minimum of £10 for any second-time parking offence with increased penalties to riders who continue to engage in high risk behaviour (i.e. temporary block, further fines). 

# *Data*

* _Risk:_ We are required to provide real-time API access (Schedule 1 clause 4.7(b)). *This data may be shared with other public authorities, including Transport for London, London Councils and neighbouring boroughs without Bolt’s consent (Schedule 1 clause 4.7(d)).* 
* _Impact: loss of competitive insight if usage data is shared widely. Also exposes our proprietary operational data (fleet algorithms, deployment patterns)._
* _Suggestion: enter into a data sharing agreement in accordance with Schedule 1 clause 4.7(e), require the Council to give notice before any data is shared, require any onward sharing to be anonymised and aggregated._ 

# *Confidential information* 

* _Risk:_ although any commercially sensitive information shared with the Council will be treated as confidential in accordance with the terms of the agreement, note that the *terms of the agreement themselves are not confidential* and may be disclosed by the Council in the interests of transparency (Schedule 1 clause 3).

** We must remove non-compliant bikes within *1 hour* (if parked in a way that causes a danger or obstruction) or *4 hours* (if parked outside agreed parking locations but not causing danger or obstruction). 
** Failure to remove a bike within the timeframes may lead to removal by the Council/Police and we will be liable for the cost of removal and storage. 
** If we receive three written warnings within a one-month period, the Council will revoke our permission to operate and remove our bikes from the area. 
* *Clause 4.3:* 
** We must always have a minimum of 50% of the permitted maximum fleet deployed in each operational zone at the beginning of each day (0600 hours). 
** The Council may amend operational zones, priority areas, or no-riding areas with 48 hours’ notice. 
* *Clause 4.4*
** Maintenance regimes of the bikes must include spot checking after every battery change, regular and pro-active inspection for wear and tear, a strategy and process for maintaining and recycling of electric batteries. 
** Note the timescales for repair/removal of bikes under clause 4.4(e) and check that these are acceptable in practice. 
* *Clause 4.5*
** Note that we are required to enforce penalties on riders who engage in high-risk behaviour and non-compliant parking - such penalties must be set at a minimum of £10 for any second-time parking offence with increased penalties to riders who continue to engage in high risk behaviour (i.e. temporary block, further fines). 

# *Data*

* _Risk:_ We are required to provide real-time API access (Schedule 1 clause 4.7(b)). *This data may be shared with other public authorities, including Transport for London, London Councils and neighbouring boroughs without Bolt’s consent (Schedule 1 clause 4.7(d)).* 
* _Impact:_ loss of competitive insight if usage data is shared widely. Also exposes our proprietary operational data (fleet algorithms, deployment patterns).
* _Suggestion:_ enter into a data sharing agreement in accordance with Schedule 1 clause 4.7(e), require the Council to give notice before any data is shared, require any onward sharing to be anonymised and aggregated. 

# *Confidential information* 

* _Risk:_ although any commercially sensitive information shared with the Council will be treated as confidential in accordance with the terms of the agreement, note that the *terms of the agreement themselves are not confidential* and may be disclosed by the Council in the interests of transparency (Schedule 1 clause 3). 

As mentioned above, once you have reviewed the risks, please let us know if you would like us to mark-up the agreement with any proposed changes. 

Best wishes

Hello,

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] with the correct user ID 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt or previous failed payment that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

I would stick to the point raised in previous conversions:
I do not see a major risk for Bolt because our actions would be supported by:
_a. Bolt calling the users only in exceptional cases with critical speeding. Meaning the situations where we are confident that driver is already putting his life, life of others and property under significant risk and we want to prevent. _b. Its driver's ultimate responsibility to ensure safe answer to the call in accordance with local traffic rules, either by using a hands free or parking the car. To your previous point [@aleksandr.laansoo|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U05AM2HE04D] - my comments about the risks apply both to robocalls or human calls placed during the speeding event.

My view on your comments [@andrei.dementjev|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U079RBKUTNY]:

a. Using the feature only in cases of critical speeding does reduce the overall risk and gives Bolt a potential line of defence. But I don’t think it removes the risk. The main issue IMO refers to edge cases, where a call directly or indirectly contributes to an accident. It may never happen, but if it does I don’t think we’d be in a strong position to argue that Bolt played no role. Bolt would have designed a process to place calls during moments of dangerous driving, even if well-intentioned.

b. Fair points. However, that doesn’t eliminate the fact that Bolt implemented a process to call users during critical speeding events. Courts or regulators, and specially media outlets, may focus less on what the driver was doing wrong and more on whether Bolt’s action (e.g., placing a call at that moment) created a foreseeable distraction. That’s where potential liability could arise, even if partial.

I’m not too worried about users complaining about the feature. Rather the risks edge cases may expose Bolt to. This isn’t really about disputing the severity of the driver’s behaviour, but whether Bolt’s method of intervention could be seen as contributing to an accident. As a rule of thumb, liability is more likely when one affirmatively intervenes, as opposed to passively allowing a risk to play out. I think it would be very difficult to argue that Bolt breached a duty by not calling a driver during a critical speeding event, especially when the law already places the burden of safe driving clearly on the driver.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt partners with various entities as part of its Rewards program. Ordinarily, this involves sharing the driver’s data with the partner. However, sometimes it works the other way around (i.e. only the partner shares data with Bolt).
* Poland Ops wants to know ‘where we stand’ in situations where the partner shares emails / phone numbers of the partner’s customers that purchased Bolt’s services using a discount code (so that we can match this with ur own database).
** Purpose here is so that Bolt can have detailed reports to measure the effectiveness of the program. Bolt would not be sharing this data outside of the company.

+*THOUGHTS*+

* Overall risk profile = {color:#36b37e}*Low*{color}.
* *Key Risk 1:* Parter sharing the data lawfully.
** Ideally, we would want to ensure that the manufacturer has relied on an *appropriate legal basis* for sharing the data in the first place, and that it has been appropriately *transparent* with its customers about the data sharing.
*** The manufacturer would be more ‘on the hook’ here for non-compliance, but if not shared appropriately then Bolt could get some flack from disgruntled users demanding its deletion.
** An agreement with the manufacturer (with warranties) would be the most robust approach here. If this is not feasible, then asking the manufacturer for proof would count as decent due diligence.
* *Key Risk 2*: Partner marketing the offer legally.
** Presumably the partner will be marketing Bolt’s services in providing the discount code to its customers. Poland is a high-risk jurisdiction regarding marketing, and so the manufacturer can only do so with customer consent. If the manufacturer fails to do this, Bolt culd possibly be held jointly liable.
** An agreement with the manufacturer (with warranties) would be the most robust approach here. If this is not feasible, then asking the manufacturer for proof would count as decent due diligence.
** NB. Technically, such data is not explicitly covered in our privacy notice, but we could argue it if we had to.
* *Key Risk 3*: Data minimisation.
** It is worth checking if we strictly need both email address and telephone number. If only one of these is needed, we should only ask for one. This would lower the risk profile.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Do we strictly need both email address and phone number to check the relevant users? Would sending the codes not be enough?
** Presumably the effectiveness reports would be aggregated (i.e., number of users that redeemed the codes)?
** Presumably the partner will be marketing Bolt’s services to its customers? If so, do we currently have any visibility on the marketing comms / how the partner ensures that such marketing is done legally?
* Subject to the above, provided the data is strictly necessary, we are ok to do this. But it would be preferable to take one of the following two approaches to protect Bolt’s position. If we do not, these is a residual non-compliance risk.
** (a) Enter into an agreement with the manufacturer and insert DP warranties.
** (b) Conduct DD on the manufacturer to check everything is in order.
* We should also ensure we anonymise the data on our end when we no longer need user-specific info.

Thanks [~accountid:712020:968f9b18-e4cc-4bff-b0fd-f9b52cc452f0] - The data exchange that you have described (i.e., the partner sharing email addresses and phone numbers with Bolt) is something we {color:#36b37e}+*can*+{color} do, as this is overall low risk  ✅ 

+*However*+, given that Poland is a high-risk country when it comes to promotional activities (which are always a part of Bolt Rewards), there are certain steps we should take to protect Bolt’s position when this sharing takes place ⚠️ 

I have set out a full breakdown of what is needed below, but {color:#4c9aff}*in summary*{color}: 💡 

# Assuming that we are entering into an agreement with the partner, there are some *pro-Bolt provisions* that I would like to insert; and
# We should ensure that the partner is only sharing ‘*strictly necessary*’ data with us, which is *subsequently* *aggregated* when we compile the effectiveness reports.

----

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Risk 1: Sharing the data lawfully*
{panel}

*Issue*: In order to share the customer contact details with us, the partner must do so lawfully (i.e., complying with data privacy laws). If the partner fails to do this, then it will be primarily the partner (not Bolt) that is ‘on the hook’ for any non-compliance - however, we may still be required to then delete the data on our side if it turns out it was shared unlawfully. This would result in operational friction and possible liability exposure. We must therefore ensure we have a redress mechanism if this were to happen.

*Solution*: Assuming that we will enter into an agreement with the partner, we should *insert some data privacy warranties / indemnities* so that we can recover from the partner if anything goes wrong in this context. I would be happy to prepare them if we reach that stage.

* Alternatively, if we do not contract with the partner (which is obviously a riskier approach), we should at least ask them to provide proof that they are sharing the contact details lawfully, have appropriate privacy notices in place, etc. Again, I can assist with this if needed.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Risk 2: Direct marketing*
{panel}

*Issue*: Given that the partner will be providing Bolt discount codes to its customers, presumably it will also be marketing Bolt’s services to these customers, right? If so, then it is important that the partner has obtained the customer’s consent to send them marketing materials. If the partner fails to do this, then it will be primarily the partner that is ‘on the hook’ for any non-compliance - however, there have been cases in Poland where the party that is promoted in the marketing (which in this case would be Bolt) is also held liable. We must therefore ensure we have a redress mechanism if this were to happen.

*Solution*: Assuming that we will enter into an agreement with the partner, we should *insert some data privacy warranties / indemnities* so that we can recover from the partner if anything goes wrong in this context. I would be happy to prepare them if we reach that stage.

* Alternatively, if we do not contract with the partner (which is obviously a riskier approach), we should at least ask them to provide proof that they are obtaining consent from their customers, as well as what measures they have in place if a customer withdraws their consent.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Risk 3: Data minimisation*
{panel}

*Issue*: Under applicable privacy laws, we should only be exchanging data that is ‘strictly necessary’. If we need both the email address and the phone number of the customer to identify them on our systems, then that is fine. However, if we can achieve the same purpose with less, then we should aim to exchange less data.

*Solution*: If we can still identify the customers on our systems with, for example, just the phone number (or eve just the discount code itself), then ideally we should only be exchanging that data. However, if we need both email address and phone numbers, this is something we can do.

* Additionally, I assume that once we receive this data, the reports themselves will only contain aggregated statistics (i.e., the number of users that have used the discounts) rather than details of specific users? If so, this is good - we should delete the data we have received from the partner once we no longer need it.

Thank you for escalating. This case qualifies as a personal data breach resulting from phone number recycling, which allowed a new user to access an existing rider account (and vice versa). 

Please take the following actions *immediately* to contain and close the incident:

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. Required actions
{panel}

# *Confirm the root cause*

* Review the rider account in Admin Panel and verify that two different devices accessed the same account using the same phone number, confirming number recycling.
* Document the findings in the internal note before proceeding with containment.

# *Contain the breach*

* Archive the compromised account immediately once confirmation is obtained.
** If archival is blocked due to an outstanding debt, raise a Fraud Team Service Desk ticket requesting debt forgiveness, citing:
“Account accessed by another person due to phone number recycling, breach containment required as per Privacy Legal.”
** Proceed with archival once debt is cleared.
* Ensure all active sessions are logged out prior to archival.

# *Notify both impacted users*

* *To the new number owner:* inform that their account will be archived and they should create a new account using the same number.
* *To the original number owner:* explain that the account linked to their old number was accessed due to number recycling, has now been archived, and they can re-register securely. Add an apology line reflecting that the issue was resolved with delay and that no further access will occur.

h3. 1️⃣ Message to the *new number owner*

_(Send via the in-app channel or verified contact on file.)_

{quote}Dear [Name],

Our investigation shows that your phone number ending in [{color:#ff5630}last 4 digits{color}] was previously linked to another Bolt account. This can occur when mobile operators recycle numbers that are no longer in use. When a number is reassigned, the new owner may inadvertently gain access to the previous account connected to that number.

To protect your and the other user’s data, we will now archive this account. Once archived, neither you nor the previous owner will be able to access it. You can immediately create a new Bolt account using your current phone number, this will ensure your new account is fully secure and linked only to you.

To keep your account secure in the future, please make sure that:

* Your phone number and email address in the app are up to date;
* You verify your email address;
* You enable Two-Step Verification in the Bolt app under _My account → Log in and security_; and
* You never share your one-time password (OTP) or passkey with anyone.

We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience. Please rest assured that your new account will not contain any information belonging to another user.{quote}



h3. 2️⃣ Message to the *original account holder*

_(Send via email address listed in Account Details History.)_

{quote}Dear [Name],

Our records show that your Bolt account associated with the phone number ending in [{color:#bf2600}last 4 digits{color}] was recently accessed by another person. This occurred because your old phone number was reassigned by your mobile operator and remained linked to your Bolt account. The new number owner inadvertently gained access when they tried to create their own account.

We have now archived your old account to ensure that no one else can access your personal information (including your ride history, addresses, and invoices). If you would like to continue using Bolt, please create a new account using your current phone number and verified email address.

To protect your new account, please ensure that:

* Your contact details are always up to date;
* Your email is verified;
* You enable Two-Step Verification via _My account → Log in and security_; and
* You do not share your OTP or passkey with anyone.

We apologise for the delay in resolving this issue.{quote}



# *Update internal systems*

* Add a clear Beehive note linking both users’ cases.
* Mark the case as _contained_ once both communications have been sent and account archival confirmed.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
h3. Additional notes
{panel}

Do *not* delete the account manually - use the archival procedure to preserve audit trail.

Hi [~accountid:620e4df5a713ab0068139e4a], thank you for providing the Confidentiality Agreement. I have now reviewed this against Bolt’s template mutual NDA (attached for your reference) and have set out my {color:#ff5630}*concerns*{color} below. I have also included a {color:#36b37e}*resolution*{color} for each of these concerns by way of marking-up the attached Confidentiality Agreement.

# *Scope and purpose*

* {color:#ff5630}Concern{color}: Bolt’s NDA references a general “Relationship” or discussions about a possible relationship whereas DA’s is specific to “working together to obtain further detail of Bolt’s operations at Dublin Airport.” DA’s version is narrow — protection only applies to info shared _for this defined purpose_, leaving room for argument that other disclosures (e.g., operational data shared later) are outside scope.
* {color:#36b37e}Resolution{color}: I have broadened the scope to include all information shared “in connection with discussions or commercial relationships between the parties.”

# *Definition of Confidential Information*

* {color:#ff5630}Concern{color}: DA’s agreement requires that oral disclosures must later be confirmed in writing and marked “CONFIDENTIAL.” DA’s definition narrows protection — unconfirmed oral or unmarked information may not be protected.
* {color:#36b37e}Resolution{color}: I have removed that requirement.

# *Use and disclosure restrictions*

* {color:#ff5630}Concern{color}: DA’s agreement adds an express right for DA to disclose information to Irish government departments (Department of Transport / Department of Public Expenditure and Reform) without requiring consent (Clause 3.3) There is no reciprocal right for Bolt. This creates an uneven disclosure regime and weakens Bolt’s confidentiality protection — particularly concerning sensitive operational or financial information.
* {color:#36b37e}Resolution{color}: I have included that any such public body disclosures are subject to prior notice and limited to what is legally required and Bolt retains the right to seek protective measures before disclosure.

# *Return or destruction of information*

* {color:#ff5630}Concern{color}: DA’s agreement adds that a recipient may retain copies for regulatory or compliance purposes which could allow retention of Bolt’s data indefinitely under vague “regulatory” justification.
* {color:#36b37e}Resolution{color}: I have amended this to only legal purposes.

# *Liability cap*

* {color:#ff5630}Concern{color}: Bolt’s NDA includes no liability cap, whereas DA’s agreement caps liability at €50,000 total for any breach (Clause 9). This significantly limits DA’s exposure if it breaches confidentiality, but limits Bolt’s ability to recover damages. This is highly disadvantageous for Bolt.
* {color:#36b37e}Resolution{color}: I have removed this cap in the first instance. However, if DA reject this amendment, we can look to increase the cap.

# *Assignment and affiliates*

* {color:#ff5630}Concern{color}: DA’s agreement prohibits assignment without written consent. This restricts flexibility for Bolt’s corporate structure.
* {color:#36b37e}Resolution{color}: I have removed the need for consent (as in Bolt’s NDA).

# *Term / duration*

* {color:#ff5630}Concern{color}: DA’s duration is much shorter (1 year rather than 3 years). This means Bolt’s confidential information could lose protection after 12 months.
* {color:#36b37e}Resolution{color}: I have increased this to 3 years minimum post-termination.



In terms of next steps, please let me know your thoughts on my proposed amendments and we can then look to negotiate these with Dublin Airport. Please let me know if you have any questions 🙂

Hi [~accountid:712020:39862b6a-cbb6-48d3-bbfa-fb7eef30bf81], I have now reviewed the changes that 6sense made to our NDA and my summary is set out below. 

In short, *there are no issues with accepting these changes, asides from the governing law (clause 12).* 

*Clause 7*

* Change made: including that any actions that the Disclosing Party takes in order to protect its information, following a notification from the Receiving Party that they will be sharing the information in accordance with a mandatory disclosure (clause 5), will be at the Disclosing Party’s expense.
* Opinion: I think this is fair and reasonable to accept - this does not impose a high risk to Bolt. :green-check: 

*Clause 9*

* Change made: including that a party seeking an injunction does *not* need to (a) prove actual or likely damages (showing why money alone wouldn’t be enough) and (b) post a bond or security to protect the other party if the injunction later turns out to have been wrongly granted.
* Opinion: Since the NDA is mutual, both parties have equal benefit from this clause if they are the disclosing party. It slightly increases the risk that 6sense could seek an injunction against Bolt without proving damages or posting security — but that risk is theoretical unless Bolt breaches the NDA and is low. :green-check: 

*Clause 10*

* Change made: Increasing the period that confidential information survives post-termination from 3 years to 5 years.
* Opinion: *This actually enhances Bolt’s protection* as it ensures that 6sense must maintain confidentiality for longer. :green-check: 

*Clause 11*

* Change made: Amending the warranty clause so that it is mutual.
* Opinion: This is acceptable provided that the NDA is mutual. :green-check: 

*Clause 12*

* Change made: {color:#ff5630}Amending the governing law from Estonian law to Delaware law.{color} (x) 
* Opinion: If possible, we should push back on this one and insist on *Estonian law* because it aligns with Bolt’s place of incorporation, avoids unnecessary U.S. legal exposure and cost, and ensures practical enforceability. If 6sense do not accept Estonian law, we should opt for *UK law* as a neutral law.

-I’ve used below sql to find out the difference between- *-service fee records-* -and- *-service fee invoice row-*-, and only taking the difference from 0.0001 up to 0.20 that can be occurred due to rounding.-


{noformat}WITH service_fee_invoiced AS (
    SELECT 
        d.to_agent_id AS company_id,
        ROUND(SUM(r.sum_with_vat), 2) AS service_fee_invoiced_sum,
        d.currency
    FROM 
        glue.ng_public.billing_document_invoice_document AS d
    LEFT JOIN 
        glue.ng_public.billing_document_invoice_document_row AS r 
    ON 
        r.invoice_id = d.id
    WHERE 
        d.system_type = 'business' 
        AND d.invoice_type IN ('business_bolt_company_monthly_invoice', 'business_bolt_company_monthly_statement') 
        AND r."type" = 'fee'
        AND d.to_agent_type = 'business_company'
        AND d.is_active = true
        AND d.created > DATE '2024-06-03'
    GROUP BY 
        d.to_agent_id, d.currency
),
service_fee_records AS (
    SELECT 
        from_agent_id AS company_id,
        SUM(sum_with_vat) AS non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum,
        currency
    FROM 
        ng_public.business_invoicing_record
    WHERE 
        type IN ('service_fee') 
        AND is_active = true
        AND created > DATE '2024-06-03'
    GROUP BY 
        from_agent_id, currency
)
SELECT 
    sfr.company_id,
    sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum,
    sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum,
    sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum AS service_fee_adjustment_amount,
    bc.balance AS current_balance,
    bc.balance + (sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum) AS balance_after_service_fee_adjustment,
    -- Check if adjustment will round the balance or not
    CASE 
        WHEN ROUND(bc.balance + (sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum), 2) 
             = bc.balance + (sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum)
        THEN 'YES'
        ELSE 'NO'
    END AS will_service_fee_adjustment_round_the_balance,
    -- Additional amount needed to round to 2 decimal places
    CASE 
        WHEN ROUND(bc.balance + (sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum), 2) 
             = bc.balance + (sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum)
        THEN 0.00  -- Already rounded to 2 decimals
        ELSE 
            ROUND(bc.balance + (sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum), 2)
            - (bc.balance + (sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum))
    END AS additional_adjustment_amount_to_round_the_balance,
    -- Total adjustment (service fee + rounding adjustment)
    (sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum) + 
    CASE 
        WHEN ROUND(bc.balance + (sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum), 2) 
             = bc.balance + (sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum)
        THEN 0.00
        ELSE 
            ROUND(bc.balance + (sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum), 2)
            - (bc.balance + (sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum))
    END AS total_adjustment_amount,
    sfr.currency
FROM 
    service_fee_records AS sfr
JOIN 
    service_fee_invoiced AS sfi
ON 
    sfr.company_id = sfi.company_id
JOIN 
    ng_public.business_invoicing_business_company AS bc
ON 
    bc.id = sfi.company_id
WHERE 
    sfr.non_rounded_service_fee_records_sum - sfi.service_fee_invoiced_sum BETWEEN 0.0001 AND 0.20
ORDER BY service_fee_adjustment_amount ASC;{noformat}

{code:python}df_order_data = spark.sql(
    """
with business_orders as 
(
	select *,
		(bb_total_fee_sum - (gmv_price_diff - COALESCE(voucher_price, 0))) AS profit_proxy
	from
	(
		select 
			order_id,
			user_id,
			entity_id,
			city_id,
			order_created_local_date,
			gmv_eur,
			gmv_eur_without_service_fee,
			price_eur_without_service_fee,
			service_fee,
			total_fee_sum,
			targeted_bonus,
			--voucher_price,
			--total_fee_sum+service_fee-targeted_bonus as profit_proxy, -- old wrong calculation with targeted_bonus
			--ebpom.total_fee_sum as total_fee_sum, -- for exchange rate calculation
			GREATEST(ebpom.gmv_eur_without_service_fee - ebpom.price_eur_without_service_fee, 0) AS gmv_price_diff, -- for exchange rate calculation
			ROUND(ebpom.voucher_price / currency.rate, 4) AS voucher_price, -- for exchange rate calculation
            (ebpom.service_fee + ebpom.total_fee_sum) AS bb_total_fee_sum, -- for exchange rate calculation
			--ebpom.gmv_eur_without_service_fee as gmv_eur 
				case when is_portal then 'TA' when is_wp then 'WP' else null end wp_ta, 
				case when product='team account - new portal'  or product='team account - old portal' or product='work profile' or product='ridebooker - cash' or product='cash ridebooker - API' or product='ridebooker - team account' or  product='ridebooker - old portal' or product='team account - API' or product='team account - voucher' or product='business delivery' or product='ridebooker - delivery' then 'RH'
					when product='rental - business' or  product='rental - wp' then 'Rental'
					when product='carsharing - business' or product='carsharing - wp' or product='carsharing - long term rental' then 'Carsharing'
					when product='business food'  then 'Food' 
				end as vertical
			from ng_public_spark.etl_business_product_order_metrics as ebpom
			/* Exchange rate join path (company → city → country → currency → rate on order date) */
			LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.etl_business_business_company AS bbc
			ON ebpom.entity_id = bbc.id
			LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_city AS company_city
			ON company_city.id = bbc.city_id
			LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_country AS company_country
			ON company_country.code = company_city.country_code
			LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.currency_exchange_rates AS currency
			ON company_country.currency = currency.currency
			AND ebpom.order_created_local_date = currency.valid_on

			where ebpom.finished_orders = 1
			and ebpom.order_created_local_date >= date('{0}') and  ebpom.order_created_local_date <= date('{1}')
	) 
)
  select *
  from business_orders
  where wp_ta='TA' and vertical='RH'
""".format(start,end)
).toPandas(){code}

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Thank you for contacting us with your inquiry regarding the handling of your personal data, specifically concerning whether Bolt engages in the selling or sharing of user information.

We wish to state clearly that Bolt does not sell users' personal data, including location data, to any third parties in exchange for monetary consideration or other forms of commercial gain. This has consistently been our approach to user data.

In the course of providing and optimising our services, it is necessary for us to process certain personal data. Data protection law permits such processing for legitimate operational purposes. This processing may involve sharing or transferring data with specific categories of recipients, including other companies within the Bolt Group and trusted third-party partners who assist us in performing essential functions necessary for service delivery and improvement.

*Data from other sources*
In limited circumstances, Bolt also receives data from external sources:

* Fraud prevention: we use a service provided by _IPQualityScore_ to analyse IP address data. This helps us identify and prevent potentially fraudulent activity on our platform.
* Marketing optimisation: we receive aggregated or pseudonymised data from advertising platforms such as Google and Meta, as well as from our mobile measurement partner. This information allows us to assess the effectiveness of our advertising campaigns and optimise our marketing spend. Importantly, these partners do not share information that directly identifies individual riders.

No personally identifiable rider data is received from these partners, and all processing is conducted strictly in line with applicable data protection laws.

*Use of location data*
When you use the Bolt app, we collect precise or approximate location data (such as GPS and IP address) to facilitate ride matching, calculate fares, and ensure safe and efficient journeys. The legal basis for processing this information is the performance of the contract (to enable your ride and ensure accurate pricing) and legitimate interest (to enhance service reliability and safety). You may choose to disable location sharing through your device settings, but this may limit certain app functionalities.

All processing activities, including any sharing or transfer of personal data, are carried out securely and in compliance with applicable data protection laws. We apply appropriate technical and organisational measures to safeguard your personal data.

*Your rights*
In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request rectification, erasure, restriction of processing, or to object to processing. You may also lodge a complaint with your local data protection authority if you are dissatisfied with our handling of your personal data.

If you have additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.

Kind regards,
Bolt{quote}

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba
