Hi [~accountid:712020:338dfd87-ef5d-40bb-b10d-871b880aa66d] Thiago’s input is correct. 

* When a full, partial refund or compensation is given to a customer, we first ask where they want to receive it. There is a pop up banner that says Bolt Balance: immediately / Original payment method (2-5 working days/something like that). Is not that we offer to refund users via Bolt Balance but they have the right to refuse, the correct way to put it is that we give them the option to choose. 
* Any amounts made available in Bolt Balance are no longer refundable or redeemable. Meaning once the user has chose to be refunded or compensated via Bolt Balance, Bolt Balance T&Cs apply and they cannot ask for these funds to be transferred to their bank account or sent back to their card.
* If a user choses refund to their original payment method, it simply should go back to the source bank account. We do not offer a transfer or refund to payment methods/accounts other than the source of the respective payment being refunded. 

So to answer the question: {color:#4c9aff}Is there any blocker from legal perspective that would prevent us from offering Bolt Balance as first option as refund? {color}
As mentioned, if the user is entitled to a full or partial refund, where to get it should be the users choice and not offered as a first option.

Comments received (under review):

* *_Scheduled rides – principal risk:_* _Bolt accepts Rider bookings well in advance but only offers them to Drivers shortly before the ride. This means Bolt commits to fulfil the booking before securing a Driver, suggesting principal behaviour under IFRS 15. The risk is reinforced by marketing (e.g., “car will be waiting” for airport pick-ups), implying Bolt, not the Driver, makes the performance promise._
* *_Late payment interest – constructive obligation:_* _The T&Cs allow charging late interest, but this is not applied in practice. Consistent non-enforcement could create a constructive obligation or weaken Bolt’s position if challenged. This is not an issue from IFRS perspective, just highlighting that actual practise differs from T&Cs._
* *_Rider promotions – missing clause:_* _The draft omits the previous clause stating that if a Passenger fare is discounted, Bolt compensates the Driver for the reduction. This creates uncertainty on who bears the cost of Rider promotions and may affect revenue recognition. For reference, previous versions of the T&Cs included this: “If the Fare paid by the Passengers is reduced as part of such campaign, we shall pay you compensation amounting to the monetary value of the benefit offered to the Passengers.”_
* *_Credit risk – constructive obligation:_* _Although the T&Cs say Bolt pays Drivers only after collecting from Riders, in practice Bolt prepays Drivers. This exposes Bolt to Rider credit risk and, over time, could create a constructive obligation and support a view that Bolt acts as principal in substance._

As you can see, the legal requirement emphasises meal-based allowances rather than time-based conditions. Therefore, employees should be able to select which meal allowance they wish to claim (Breakfast, Lunch, Dinner).

This daily allowance applies to both domestic and overseas travel. For domestic day-to-day travel, employees might not always stay in a hotel but could still claim allowances for specific meals depending on their circumstances. Thus, we cannot automatically apply breakfast to everyone by default.

To ensure consistency with our policy (which allows breakfast allowances regardless whether it was inclusive to their stay), I propose enabling two allowance items:

*Domestic travel:* Employees manually select which meals they consumed (Breakfast, Lunch, Dinner).

*Overseas travel:* The system pre-fills 100% of the rate for days with a full 24-hour duration (based on trip duration requested to fill). For partial travel days, employees can manually tick the relevant meal boxes they wish to claim

If meals (e.g., lunch or dinner) were provided, employees can untick those options accordingly. In this category, we could disable unticking option from breakfast

This approach keeps the configuration simple while enabling feasible user experience and maintaining compliance, fairness, and ethical responsibility by allowing employees to self-declare their meal claims accurately.

Happy to hear if you or the FinTech team see any constraints with this setup.

{quote}_... in PL RTA is very specific in prescribing that rides have to be performed personally by the driver who accepted the ride ...._{quote}

As always, what matters most is the most obvious interpretation under local language and laws.

Based on the English translation of the [RTA|https://lexlege.pl/ustawa-o-transporcie-drogowym/], there seems to be fair room to argue that driver-to-driver substitution mid-order is possible. From a safety perspective, there’s no real difference between:

* driver A handing over the order to driver B mid-ride
* driver A cancelling and Bolt reassigning the same ride to driver B^^^ In both cases, Bolt enables the transport assignment to be completed by driver B. What matters is that Bolt knows who the active driver is, which would always be true.

Saying substitution is _not_ possible when lobbying is a bit of a gamble (high risk, high reward). On one hand, it’s great if that helps exclude substitution from presumption criteria, although that seems unlikely considering appointing substitutes is a key part of the [Yodel Criteria|https://www.lewissilkin.com/insights/2020/04/30/employment-status-ecj-clarifies-who-counts-as-a-worker-under-eu-law-in-gig-economy-ruling]. On the other, it gives up our ability to make the argument elsewhere, and saying “we can’t do it” could look shaky compared with other markets.

Further, section 6 of the RTA appears to expressly enable substitution (see screenshot).

Thanks [~accountid:60ab8fc8efa79d00691a340f] - I have taken a look and, in short, this is {color:#ff5630}+*riskier*+{color} than the previous proposal (due to potential marketing issues) ⚠️ 

Nevertheless, I understand the importance of promoting Flex to UK drivers. As such, it is open to the business to go ahead with this proposal, but in order to do so, we would need to ensure that: (i) sensible mitigation measures are used; and (ii) the business is happy to accept the risk. In particular: 💡 

# *_We should ideally check whether the offboarded drivers have previously: (a) asked to delete their contact information / personal data; and/or (b) unsubscribed from Bolt marketing emails (or communications from Bolt in general). If they have, we should NOT contact them._*
# *_All such emails should contain a clear ‘unsubscribe’ option, which can be honoured on our side if selected by the driver._*
# *_We should ideally not contact drivers who have been offboarded for longer than 6 months._*

I include further details below. Happy to discuss if any of this is unclear. I would also invite [~accountid:712020:209f6e12-e421-4fbf-9a9f-60d100117bab]'s views on this, given the discussions we previously had on this ticket 🙂 

----

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*(1) Previous deletion requests* 
{panel}

⚠️ *Issue*: As with my previous advice on the ticket, there is a risk here that we may be reaching out to drivers that are under the impression that we have deleted their personal data (e.g., because they submitted a data deletion request before being offboarded). If we reach out to such drivers, they may believe that we are retaining and using their contact information unlawfully, which could result in driver complaints / escalation risk.

✅ *Mitigations*: As previously mentioned, it would be helpful to {color:#36b37e}*check (before contacting the driver) whether they have previously submitted an erasure request*{color} in relation to their account / personal data (and if they had, we should ideally not contact them). If this is not operationally feasible, then it is up to the business whether it wants to accept this risk.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*(2) Direct marketing*
{panel}

⚠️ *Issue*: Unlike the previous scenario, it may be difficult to characterise these emails as purely _service_-related messages - instead, they are likely to qualify as *_direct marketing_* under UK laws, given that they are ‘promoting’ Bolt Flex. Ordinarily, such laws state that we can only send promotional emails to drivers where we have their consent to do so - this seems impractical for drivers that have been offboarded for 6+ months. However, we may be able to send these emails _without_ the driver’s consent (relying on something known as the ‘soft opt-in’ exemption) if certain criteria are met. As such, they key issue here is *_whether we can argue that we meet these criteria_* - otherwise, we could face regulatory investigation and potential enforcement / fines. In particular:

* +Condition 1+: We must be promoting ‘similar’ products/services to what Bolt previously provided to the driver.
** We could of course try to argue that Bolt Flex falls under the ‘ride-hailing’ umbrella and therefore this offering is similar to what the driver was previously doing. However, given that the whole point of Bolt Flex is to position it is different to the principal model, this argument could pose a risk to how we are characterising Bolt Flex overall (cc. [~accountid:712020:209f6e12-e421-4fbf-9a9f-60d100117bab]).
* +Condition 2+: The driver must have been given the opportunity to opt out of these comms since their email address was first collected, and in all subsequent communications.
** In its most basic form, this means that any emails that we send to the offboarded drivers must contain an ‘unsubscribe’ option. This should not be controversial to implement (provided that it is still possible to implement for _offboarded_ users), since we already have unsubscribe processes in place.
** More problematically, however, is where a driver (while they were active) unsubscribed to receiving marketing comms from Bolt, and were then subsequently offboarded. We would likely not be permitted under direct marketing laws to promote Bolt Flex to such drivers, and so it is important to check which ones have already unsubscribed.
* +Condition 3+: The driver must not otherwise have a good reason to assume that their consent should have been collected for sending them these kinds of comms.
** The longer the driver has been offboarded for, the weaker our arguments for not relying on consent become (as drivers who have not been driving for Bolt for years would not expect to receive these kinds of messages). The same goes for if we have in any way given the driver the impression that our arrangement with them is permanently terminated.
** Additionally, if we previously obtained the driver’s consent for sending this kind of marketing comms (I doubt this is the case, but it is worth checking), and the driver withdrew that consent before offboarding, then we should also not be sending them these comms.

✅ *Mitigations*: If the business wants to proceed with contacting offboarded drivers about Bolt Flex, I recommend: (1) {color:#36b37e}*checking (before contacting the driver) whether they previously unsubscribed from receiving Bolt marketing* {color}or withdrew their consent to such marketing{color:#36b37e} {color}(and if they had, we should not contact them); and (2) ensuring that the emails contain an {color:#36b37e}*option to unsubscribe from receiving them*{color} (which Bolt is able to action, if selected - e.g., an ‘unsubscribe’ link); and (3) {color:#36b37e}*not contacting drivers that have been offboarded for longer than 6 months*{color} (as the longer the period, the weaker our arguments for sending these comms becomes).

👋 Hey there!
If you need a *report*, please refer to FleetX (DriverX). If your request concerns an *invoice*, follow these steps:

1. Open the **Client page in Admin**: [link|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients?tz=Europe%2FTallinn&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D].
2. Enter the Fleet or Driver ID in the **External ID** filter field.
3. Open the driver or fleet profile.
4. Go to the **Invoice tasks** tab.
   * If you see *Invoice sum too small*, no commission invoice was generated because the driver either owed no commission or had more compensation than commission.
   * If you encounter any other error, please let us know.
5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under **Invoice tasks** or **Partner Invoices**.

Best regards,
*Billing Ops AI*

👋 Hey there!
If you need a *report*, please refer to FleetX (DriverX). If your request concerns an *invoice*, follow these steps:

1. Open the **Client page in Admin**: [link|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients?tz=Europe%2FTallinn&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D].
2. Enter the Fleet or Driver ID in the **External ID** filter field.
3. Open the driver or fleet profile.
4. Go to the **Invoice tasks** tab.
   * If you see *Invoice sum too small*, no commission invoice was generated because the driver either owed no commission or had more compensation than commission.
   * If you encounter any other error, please let us know.
5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under **Invoice tasks** or **Partner Invoices**.

Best regards,

*TL:DR*

*Goal:*
Ensure consistent, accessible disabled behavior across Web (React), React Native iOS, and React Native Android.

*Definition:*
Disabled = non-interactive, visually inactive, and semantically announced – not hidden.

*Platform guidance:*

* *Web:* 
** Use {{disabled}} for non-interactive controls.
** Use {{aria-disabled="true"}} only when the element must remain focusable for context; block activation manually.
* *iOS:* 
** Use {{isEnabled = false}} for disabled controls.
** Use focusable-but-disabled ({{UIAccessibilityTraits.notEnabled}} without disabling interaction) *only when necessary*; block activation.
* *Android:* 
** Use {{setEnabled(false)}} for disabled; element is skipped in focus.
** Do *not* keep disabled elements focusable; TalkBack expects them skipped.
* *RN*: 
** {{disabled}} removes press; add {{accessibilityState={{disabled: true}}}}. 
** Focusable-but-disabled: allowed only on iOS behaviorally, but *React Native should avoid this pattern* for consistency across platforms.

*Do not disable:*
Navigation, static info, or error messages.

*Design, interaction and accessibility:*
Maintain 3:1 contrast, block focus/press for disabled, and verify announcements on VoiceOver, TalkBack, NVDA, JAWS.

*Align on:*
Visual styling, focus rules, screen reader validation and component scope.

My input on the disabled states would be:

*Definition of disabled components*

A disabled state indicates that:

* The user cannot interact with the element.
* The element is visually and functionally inactive.
* The state is communicated semantically, not just visually.

In accessibility terms, this involves ARIA and native semantics, keyboard focus handling and screen reader announcements.

----

*Disabled doesn’t mean hidden*

* Disabled elements should remain perceivable but not operable.
* They indicate potential affordances (e.g., a form field that will activate once prior fields are filled).

*Disabled doesn’t mean inaccessible*
The user must understand why something is disabled and what can be done to enable it. Provide context through helper text, tooltip, or status message.

*Avoid dead ends*
A disabled control should never be the only way to perform an essential task.

----

*Platform behaviour for disabled components/elements*

||*Platform*||*Semantics*||*Keyboard*||*VoiceOver / TalkBack / Other Screen readers*||
|Web (react)|{{disabled}} (native elements) removes interactivity and focus; {{aria-disabled="true"}} conveys disabled state but remains focusable for context.|{{disabled}}: element not focusable or interactive.
{{aria-disabled}}: element focusable, but activation must be blocked manually.|{{disabled}}: announced as “dimmed” / “unavailable.”
{{aria-disabled}}: announced as “dimmed” / “unavailable,” but element still reachable.|
|Android native|{{disabled}} blocks presses and removes focus; {{accessibilityState={{ disabled: true }}}} sets accessibility node as disabled ({{setEnabled(false)}}).|{{disabled}}: element not focusable and not interactive.
{{accessibilityState}} alone: element may remain focusable, but this is not recommended on Android.|TalkBack announces “disabled.” Disabled items are generally skipped during linear navigation; “focusable but disabled” pattern is not standard.|
|iOS native|{{disabled}} blocks press/touch events; {{accessibilityState={{ disabled: true }}}} exposes {{UIAccessibilityTraits.notEnabled}}.|{{disabled}}: element not focusable or interactive.
{{accessibilityState}} only: can remain focusable for context if desired.|VoiceOver announces “dimmed” or “not enabled.” Focus typically skips fully disabled elements unless {{accessibilityState}} is used alone.|
|React native|{{disabled={true}}} removes interactivity and prevents press events; {{accessibilityState={{ disabled: true }}}} conveys disabled state to assistive tech while remaining visible. Components should not be focusable when disabled.|Disabled elements are not focusable. Custom components must explicitly set {{focusable={false}}} when disabled.|VoiceOver and TalkBack announce disabled controls as “dimmed” / “disabled.” Element remains reachable by swipe navigation only if marked accessible, but will be announced as unavailable and cannot be activated.|

*When (and how) to keep a disabled element* *focusable for context*

Use this pattern only where it helps users understand context, such as a menu item that is visible but not yet available. Otherwise, prefer a standard disabled (non-focusable) control.

*Web react*

* *How:* Use {{aria-disabled="true"}} on an element with the right role. Keep it focusable ({{tabIndex=0}} if needed), and block activation in handlers.
* *Why:* {{aria-disabled}} communicates the state to screen readers but doesn’t change behavior.

*iOS native*

* *How (case-by-case):* Prefer standard disabled, but if context is important, do not set {{disabled}}. Use {{accessibilityState={{ disabled: true }}}} so VoiceOver announces “dimmed,” and block activation in {{onPress}}/{{onKeyDown}}.
* *Why:* This keeps the item in the VO navigation order for context, but you must prevent action yourself.

*Android native*

*Guidance:* Avoid focusable-but-disabled. TalkBack users expect disabled items to be skipped. Use {{disabled}} (and {{accessibilityState={{ disabled: true }}}}) so it’s non-interactive and not focusable.
If context is needed, provide helper text, a tooltip, or a read-only row instead of keeping the control focusable.

*React native*

* Use {{accessibilityState={{ disabled: true }}}} on an element with the correct {{accessibilityRole}} (e.g., {{"button"}}, {{"menuitem"}}, {{"checkbox"}}).
* Keep it focusable by ensuring:
** {{focusable={true}}}, and
** the element remains {{accessible={true}}}.
* Block activation manually by omitting {{onPress}} or guarding inside the handler.
* Do not mark the component as {{disabled={true}}} – that removes interactivity and removes focusability.

----

*Don’t disable*

Avoid disabling components that are:

* Critical for navigation (primary menu links, breadcrumb links). Instead, hide or replace them if the destination is unavailable.
* Static informative elements - they don’t need a disabled state.
* Error or validation messages - must remain readable and perceivable.

----

*Common interactive component based thoughts* 

||*Component*||*Disabling allowed*||*React Web*||*iOS (VoiceOver)*||*Android (TalkBack)*||*React native*||*UX guidance*||
|Buttons|Not recommended (?)|{{disabled}} (native) removes focus & activation; {{aria-disabled="true"}} keeps focusable (block activation).|{{disabled}} blocks press; {{accessibilityState={{disabled:true}}}} announces “dimmed”.|{{disabled}} removes focus & press; add {{accessibilityState={{disabled:true}}}}.|{{disabled}} removes press; add {{accessibilityState={{disabled:true}}}}.|Prefer enabled buttons + inline validation. If unavailable, hide or explain why near the button rather than greying it out.|
|Checkbox / Radio|Sometimes|{{disabled}} (native) or {{aria-disabled}} on custom group.|Use {{disabled}} + {{accessibilityState}}.|Use {{disabled}} + {{accessibilityState}}.|{{disabled}} blocks toggle; add {{accessibilityState={{disabled:true}}}}.|Prefer not showing ineligible options; or show read-only state with helper text. If you must disable, keep label readable and explain why.|
|Text Field / Text Area|Sometimes|{{disabled}} (no focus, no edit) or {{readonly}} (focusable, selectable, no edit).|{{editable={false}}} (read-only) or component-level {{disabled}}.|{{editable={false}}} or {{disabled}}.|{{disabled}} removes focus & input; add {{accessibilityState={{disabled:true}}}}.|Prefer read-only over disabled when showing data; if entry isn’t allowed yet, show input as read-only with guidance (placeholder/helper/error), not fully disabled.|
|Tooltip|No|Always available (helps explain why something is disabled).|Always available (helps explain why something is disabled).|Always available (helps explain why something is disabled).|Always available (helps explain why something is disabled).|Don’t disable tooltips; use them to provide eligibility or next-step info.|
|Link|Not recommended|Don’t “disable”; remove {{href}} or use plain text. {{aria-disabled}} on links is confusing.|Represent as static text if not actionable; avoid faux disabled links.|Represent as static text if not actionable; avoid faux disabled links.|Remove press handler; treat as non-interactive text (no disabled state).|Prefer remove/replace with text and explain state.|
|Tabs|Sometimes|If needed, {{aria-disabled="true"}} on {{role="tab"}}; keep focusable for context, block activation.|If needed, avoid {{disabled}}; use {{accessibilityState={{disabled:true}}}} (focusable for context), block {{onPress}}.|Prefer not focusable disabled tabs; if unavailable, visually indicate and skip in focus order.|Disabled tab: remove press; add {{accessibilityState={{disabled:true}}}}.|Better UX: hide tabs you can’t access yet, or keep visible but navigable to an info panel that explains requirements.|
|Toggle|Sometimes|{{disabled}} (native) or {{aria-disabled}}|{{disabled}} + {{accessibilityState}}|{{disabled}} + {{accessibilityState}}|{{disabled}} blocks toggle; add {{accessibilityState={{disabled:true}}}}.|Often better to allow toggle and then validate with clear messaging; or lock with read-only value and explain why it can’t change now.|
|Select / Dropdown|Sometimes|{{disabled}} on native selects; {{aria-disabled}} on custom, block activation.|{{disabled}} + {{accessibilityState}}|{{disabled}} + {{accessibilityState}}|{{disabled}} removes press; add {{accessibilityState={{disabled:true}}}}.|Prefer empty/placeholder + helper text or filter out unavailable items; disable only when absolutely necessary and explain why.|
|ListItem|Sometimes|If item is actionable, use {{aria-disabled}} (focusable-only if context needed) and block activation.|If context is crucial, skip {{disabled}}, use {{accessibilityState={{disabled:true}}}}, block press.|Avoid focusable-but-disabled; use non-focusable disabled styling or remove action.|Remove press; add {{accessibilityState={{disabled:true}}}}.|Prefer non-interactive presentation or badge + helper text instead of disabling the row.|
|Snackbar|No|Always available.|Always available.|Always available.|Always available.|Never disable. It’s a message, not a control. Provide actions separately (buttons) with proper state.|

----

*Visual and interactive design*

*Color and contrast*

* Text and icons in disabled states should maintain at least 3:1 contrast against the background.
* Avoid overly low opacity that makes text unreadable.

*Focus state*

* Disabled elements are typically not focusable.
* If kept focusable for context ({{aria-disabled}} / {{accessibilityState.disabled}}), they must:
** Provide clear focus indication.
** Block activation (no click/press events).

*Screen reader*

* Always ensure the element exposes correct role and disabled state.
* Use accessibility tools (VoiceOver, TalkBack, NVDA, JAWS) to verify the announcement:
“Button, disabled” / “Switch, not enabled” / “Menu item, dimmed.”

----

*What we should align on* 

# Visual styling - make sure all components that allow disabled state have well speced out consistent design
# Focus behaviour - disabled elements should not receive focus; {{aria-disabled}} {{accessibilityState={{ disabled: true }}}} items should receive focus but not respond to activation
# Validate on multiple screen readers - VoiceOver, JAWS, TalkBack and NVDA
# Ensure React Native Android / iOS and web components convey the same semantics
# Component scope - define which components support disabled states and which don’t.

We are writing in response to your follow up request from *2 October 2025* to the data subject rights request, which was received by Bolt on *26 August 2025*.

Please see our technical explanation below.



When the Bolt Courier App is closed and you are offline, we do not collect or send your location data to our servers, nor do we store it in our databases. The App may still process your location in your device memory, for example, to determine general parameters like your country or city. This information stays only on your device and is not transmitted to Bolt.



The Android operating system may still show a message about “background location use” even when no location data is sent to us. This happens because Android detects that the App has permission to access location in the background or that it accessed it while running in memory. To reiterate, this means that the app may momentarily read your location in your device’s memory, but it does not transfer  that data anywhere. You can read more about this on the Android developer site available at: [https://developer.android.com/develop/sensors-and-location/location/permissions/background|https://developer.android.com/develop/sensors-and-location/location/permissions/background|smart-link] . 

If you prefer, you can restrict location access in your phone settings (e.g., “Allow only while using the app”), but please note this may affect how the app functions when you are online and available for deliveries.

We hope our explanation clarifies your concerns.



*Your rights*



In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws.



If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.



If you have any additional questions, please contact us by replying to this message.



Sincerely,
Bolt Privacy Team{quote}

+CO review of LCC amendments to the final version of the agreement (attached)+

*Summary of LCC amendments:* 

* general tidy-up of defined terms/address of LCC. 
* clause 9 - Maintenance and misplaced E-vehicles: 
** *Change:* cross-reference change (References to _“clauses 4 and 5”_ updated to _“clauses 4, 5 and 12.”_). 
** *Comment:* This adds a link to new general obligations under clause 12, slightly broadening compliance scope. 
* clause 12 - General obligations of the Concessionaire: 
** *Changes:* 
*** new clause 12(b) added: _“Ensure that all E-vehicles are of satisfactory quality, fit for any purpose held out by the Concessionaire, free from defects in design, material and workmanship and free from any risk to the health and welfare of Users.”_
*** clause 12(b) extended to require Bolt to _“provide the Services with reasonable care and skill”_. 
** *Comment:* This introduces a *fitness-for-purpose and safety warranty* absent before. This creates a higher standard of liability. That being said, this is standard supplier wording. 
* clause 17 - Mobilisation Plan and Exit Management Plan
** *Change:* wording revised (_“submit a new amended Exit Management Plan”_ replaced with _“submit a new or make amendments to an existing Exit Management Plan”_). 
** *Comment:* Expands LCC’s power to demand *revisions to existing Exit Management plans*, not just a new one. 
* clause 18 - Payments 
** *Changes:* 
*** Old text (_“monthly in arrears … first payment one month after Commencement Date”_) deleted.
*** New wording: _“calculate and pay the Concession Fee each calendar month in arrears throughout the Term in accordance with the provisions of Schedule 4.”_
** *Comment:* Removes fixed first-payment trigger; ties timing and method strictly to Schedule 4. This change makes sense if a payment schedule was agreed in accordance with the Tender (CO to check this point with the business). 
* clause 35 - Termination
** *Change: Clause 35.1(a):* expanded to add an express *remedy period*: _“or if remediable the material breach has not been remedied within 10 Working Days of the Authority notifying the Concessionaire of the material breach.”_
** *Comment:* narrows time to cure breach (10 days). Introduces explicit written-notice trigger. LCC gains clarity and stronger early-termination right. Not ideal, however standard for concession/supplier agreements. 
* Schedule 1 - The Services 
** *Changes:* 
*** Reference to _“ITT”_ deleted and replaced with _“Specification”._ Cross-reference change: “clauses 4 and 5” → “clauses 4, 5 and 12.”
*** *New Annex A to Schedule 1 (The Specification) added.* 
** *Comment:* aligns with addition of new clause 12 obligations. CO to check with the business that this new Annex A mirrors that which was provided/agreed during the Tender stage. 
* Schedule 4 - Concession Fee 
** *Changes:* 
*** New section 2 (“Overheads and payment of Concession Fee”) which establishes overheads limits, monthly reporting within 14 days, LCC’s right to request verification and a 14-day payment window. Add administrative and reporting duties not previously in the main payment clause. 
*** New section 3 (“Exit Costs”) added which defines “Exit Costs”, caps recovery to maximums in table, sets process/timing (3 months before expiry or 14 days post-termination) and reporting requirements. 
* Appendices/Schedules renumbered
** *Appendix 1* (“Authority’s Invitation to Tender document”) – *deleted.*
** *Appendix 2* retitled as *“Schedule 9 – The Concessionaire’s Tender.*
** *Comment:* these appear to be administrative clean-up amendments to move the tender into the schedules section. 

+Analysis+ 

Having reviewed the amendments, subject to confirmation from the business,  I am comfortable that these amendments are not ‘deal-breakers'/major red flags and can be accepted. 

+Next Steps+

* CO to flag (a) the potentially problematic and (b) operational/commercial amendments to the business and seek confirmation/approval before proceeding to signature stage. 
* Once approved, CO to (a) accept the changes, (b) tidy up formatting and (c) respond to LCC and confirm the name and email address for the signatory for Bolt.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Hi [~accountid:5f0c30effe23000022252e68] !
Our assessment regarding this topic is the following:

*Context:*

The Driver Shopping feature was introduced in 2023 with the aim of shifting the power of driver selection from the platform to the rider. It allows users to choose their preferred driver from a list of 10 nearby drivers, rather than being assigned one by the system.

As discussed in a [previous ticket|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-29222], the most valuable aspect of this feature is that it *introduces an additional stakeholder — the rider — into the relationship between Bolt and the driver*. The more stakeholders are involved (e.g. fleets, riders), the more *diluted are the elements of control and direction*, which are key to characterising an employment relationship. This structural dilution is legally beneficial for Bolt.


*Reclassification risk in PT:*

* To date, there have been *no known reclassification cases* in the ride-hailing sector in Portugal.
* The *Labour Inspectorate has not shown particular focus* on ride-hailing — although this could change, and is not something we can control.
* As mentioned previously, internal assessments estimate that enabling Driver Shopping *(without own pricing)* could *improve our legal defence by approximately 10%* in the event of a reclassification challenge.

However, the *confidence level attributed to this feature is “medium”*. This means that while it is clearly helpful, the precise extent of that benefit is unknown — as it has not yet been tested in Portuguese courts. Realistically, we estimate the legal value of the feature sits *somewhere between 0% and 20%*, depending on how courts would interpret its impact on platform control.


*Conclusion:*

Having all the above in consideration, and given that:
- There is currently *no litigation or regulatory pressure* related to reclassification in ride-hailing in Portugal; and
- The feature appears to be *limiting the deployment of other functionalities* while not bringing any benefits, as you mentioned in our meeting,

We are comfortable to conclude that this is *ultimately a business decision* and that, in our view, from a legal standpoint, we think *it is OK running the proposed A/B test.*

Please do keep us informed of the results.
Thank you!

This patterns happens in both Rider and Eater app:

* user is logged in, has a refresh token (REFRESH_TOKEN_1)
* user opens app, access token is missing ([github|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/aaa49e4ddeb9a67fde0809523fca3fe427edde99/modules/user/login-core/src/main/java/eu/bolt/client/login/domain/interactor/FetchJwtTokensUseCase.kt#L21])
* app calls /profile/auth/authenticate to get a new refresh token (REFRESH_TOKEN_2) and access token from it. This action revokes REFRESH_TOKEN_1, since we can only have one active refresh token for a login session. The app works for a while
* later, user opens app, which tries to get access token with REFRESH_TOKEN_1. Gets an error because REFRESH_TOKEN_1 is now revoked

Sometimes it leads to users being logged out, sometimes not.

Example error when token is revoked: [https://kibana-logs.elasticsearch.boltint.net/app/discover#/doc/4dd94040-4b00-11ed-a2c4-23a64d9ee89b/.ds-logs-nodejs-2025.10.14-012676?id=9V6J4ZkBT5k_800SIgHZ|https://kibana-logs.elasticsearch.boltint.net/app/discover#/doc/4dd94040-4b00-11ed-a2c4-23a64d9ee89b/.ds-logs-nodejs-2025.10.14-012676?id=9V6J4ZkBT5k_800SIgHZ]

I was looking at the task to make the *product price required* according to [DPM-2020|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/DPM-2020] when a product is active and linked to stores. My investigation revealed a usability issue on the frontend that needs to be addressed alongside the backend requirement.
*Current Context:*
Currently, a user can create an *inactive product* by completing only the *Name* and *SKU* fields. To make the product *active*, the user must link it to a list of stores and set a price for those stores.
*The Problem (UX Issue)*
The price input field is *always visible*, even when no stores are selected. If the user enters a price but has not selected any stores, the price value *silently disappears* and is never sent to the backend. This created confusion and wasted time during my testing.
*Proposed Solution*
To resolve this and make the interaction clear, I recommend implementing the following frontend validation/behavior:

# *Conditional Requirement:* If the user selects *at least one store*, the *Price* field must become *required* for submission.
# *Conditional Disablement:* If *no stores are selected*, the *Price* field should be *disabled* (or visibly hidden) to clearly indicate that a price is irrelevant at this stage.

This approach will ensure that the price is only required when it is contextually needed and will prevent users from entering data that will be silently ignored.

Campaigns for non-locals were suspended due to concern over potentially low retention. This assumption was based on the research performed on the tourist signups. Tourist campaigns were live during May’24 - Feb’25 where riders were targeted with discounts ranging from 10% - 50% ([notebook|https://bolt-incentives.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/3884586534183089?o=2472566184436351#command/7207714705549948])

Aprox half of weekly GMV is generated by non LPTC users, hence it is important to have a solid strategy on how to win this segment while remaining profitable.

# users splif: Local Tourists / Foreign Tourists (coming from Bolt countries vs non Bolt countries)/ Locals

+Summary of LCC amendments for your review+

* General tidy-up of clause cross-references and housekeeping (e.g. “ITT” has been deleted and replaced with “Specification”) and appendices restructured (e.g. Appendix 2 renamed *Schedule 9 - Concessionaire’s Tender*).

** contains a new sub-clause (b) which requires all e-vehicles to be of _“satisfactory quality, fit for purpose, free from defects and safe for users.”_; and 
** sub-clause (a) has been extended to require Bolt to _“provide the Services”_ with reasonable care and skill.
** *Impact:* although this is standard wording for supplier/concession contracts, this introduces a fitness-for-purpose and user-safety obligation; raises the maintenance and quality standard beyond “best industry practice.” 
* *clause 17* (Mobilisation and Exit Management Plan) has been amended to give LCC the right to require Bolt to submit a *new* or *amended* Exit Management Plan (or make amendments to any existing Exit Management Plan). 
** *Impact:* gives LCC more control over Exit Plan updates. 
* *clause 18* (Payments) has been amended to require Bolt to *calculate and pay* the Concession Fee _each calendar month_ in line with the payment schedule in Schedule 4. 
** *Impact:* introduces an ongoing calculation/reporting obligation tied directly to Schedule 4 mechanics. +Please review Schedule 4.+
* *clause 35* (Termination) now includes the explicit right for LCC to terminate if a *material breach is not remedied within 10 working days of notice.* 
** *Impact:* although this is standard drafting and has been inserted for completeness, note that this shortens the cure period and increases termination risk exposure if we do not remedy a breach within this timescale.  
* *Schedule 4* - Concession Fee: although LCC have not amended the structure/details of the concession fee/overheads itself, *please review Schedule 4 carefully* as LCC have made a number of amendments here, namely LCC have added new sections on: 
** *Overheads and payment process* – detailed reporting (within 14 days after month-end) and LCC verification rights.
** *Exit Costs* – defines recoverable costs, sets caps and notice process (3 months before expiry or 14 days post-termination).
** *Impact:* new reporting, accounting and exit-cost controls that must align with our tender pricing assumptions.
* *Annex to Schedule 1*: note that LCC have inserted a new Annex to Schedule 1 to set out the “Specification”. *Please check that this mirrors the Specification received by us during the Tender process.* 

+Next Steps+

* +Please confirm whether you are comfortable with accepting the above-listed changes.+
* I would be grateful for your comments +today+ if possible so that we can go back to LCC and confirm our position (i.e. whether we are happy to accept the changes and proceed with signing the agreement). Please do loop in any other team members into this as appropriate.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Customer Support Ops team member (CSO) has autofill details saved for accessing the fleet portal (details were those of a former Ops employee), specifically a mock account used to gain a better understanding of how the fleet portal operates.
* On 17 October, CSO accidentally sent the access details (presumably login details) to a fleet owner. However, it is not currently certain re whether a breach actually occurred.
** Apparently the FO had access to Bolt API, which should not be available to them. 
*** However, I am not sure this is the case - per [here|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/667900897], FO flagged they were trying to work with Bolt API integrations. Ops then stated ([here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/CH24V3144/p1760689127894459?thread_ts=1760685042.415669&cid=CH24V3144]) that there is a section called ‘API connections’ available to those at Bolt, which the FO should not be able to see. 
* In terms of mitigations, CSO has removed the autofill from their keychain, and removed access fro the link that was sent to the FO.
** CSO asked FO to provide screenshots / proof. However, FO does not have proof, and claims they managed to solve the issue.
* Incident was only escalated to me on 20 October 2025, so 72-hour deadline has effectively expired :melting_face: 

+*ANALYSIS*+

* We currently do not have enough information to confirm if a data breach actually occurred. Even if we did, the scope is unclear.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Why did the reporter have autofill details saved for a former Ops employee?
** When you say access to the ‘fleet portal’, what do you mean precisely? Is this the fleet portal as it would be accessible by the dummy user, or internal Bolt employee access to the fleet portal (similar to Admin)?
** Are you sure the autofill details were sent to the FO? What actually shows this?
** In what context did the FO mention Bolt API? Would they be able to bypass this, or would then need Okta?
** So to be clear, we have no evidence that the FO actually gained access (just that they had the potential to), and this is no longer possible in any event?

Hi Jan, thanks, I’ve clarified the main points in bullets below: 

* A legal agreement doesn’t seem necessary here. If the ad agency is simply giving a promotional voucher to Bolt for nothing in return, there is no VAT. This is the simplest solution imho
* If a legal agreement is necessary, it makes things a bit more complicated
** As written, Bolt provides data and branding rights to the ad agency in exchange for ad credits. It’s not clear how Bolt’s branding will be used or what the commercial reality is, raises data privacy issues, etc. Plus, it’s not clear if or how Bolt will use the ad credits (may be worthless if we’ve never used them to advertise and don’t plan to). I’m not sure this makes commercial sense. 
** Truly, the value of Bolt isn’t the technology itself, it’s the network of drivers and users. I recommend to setup so that Bolt is referring the ad agency to its network of drivers / facilitating sales and earn something in exchange for that referral rather than handing over it its proprietary data and branding rights to the ad agency. For example, a referral link to the ad agency website on the Bolt driver app, or a quarterly comms blast referring the ad agency, would be a reasonable commercial setup 
** In any event, because there is a reciprocal performance and a legal agreement, VAT applies, reverse charged to the ad agency. Requires valid VAT invoices to be sent by Bolt to the ad agency. 
** Last, I don’t see any need for a 10 EUR fee, this seems to be just a nominal consideration and not related to any market value. It would be taxable as well. Tbh, I would think full access to CRM data from Bolt’s network would be worth a lot more. 
* Last, wrt reclass risk - this issue is one mostly of control. Not applicable where Bolt leases tablets to drivers and drivers agree to be part of Bolt's ad network. Bolt sells drivers' tablet ad space to advertisers and earns a commission. Everyone independent 😃

Shared the following feedback [in slack|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C07K9SHJPJ7/p1760699954441209] - 

Using the driving score to automatically apply penalties or benefits counts as automated decision-making (ADM). Under GDPR, this becomes a problem if those decisions are fully automated and have a major impact on the user - like blocking someone from using Bolt Drive. That kind of decision has a clear, significant effect on the person, so regulators treat it seriously.

Charging higher rates, limiting car choices, or increasing damage liability based only on the driving score are grey areas. There’s very little guidance from regulators on how 'significant' these effects are, so we need to be cautious. If a regulator decides these actions are significant ADM, Bolt might have to:

* stop making these automated decisions entirely; or
* add a 'human in the loop' - meaning someone must manually check and approve the decision before it takes effect.

*How to minimise this risk*

# *Be transparent:* we need to show users clearly how their driving behaviour affects their score (done) and what penalties or benefits can follow (in progress).
# *Add human oversight:* give users an easy way to ask for a human review if they think their score or a penalty is wrong. This proves that Bolt isn’t making purely automated decisions (_kind of_), which lowers the ADM risk.

The key is to show that decision making process behind penalties is *not fully automated or hidden from users.*

# Yes. Bolt is permitted to share this information with the fleet (e.g. Odysse) because the driver is the fleet’s employee, and the Addendum explicitly puts the compliance and performance responsibility on the fleet

* *Odysse, as employer, is responsible for managing its employees’ performance and compliance*, including responding to any misconduct or safety issues flagged by Bolt.
* *Termination or suspension by Bolt* from the platform is a commercial and compliance matter directly affecting the service Odysse is contracted to deliver. Odysse has a right to know whether it can continue to use a given employee to deliver its contractual obligations.
* *There is no obligation for Bolt to engage directly with drivers in these cases*, as the drivers are not contracting parties to the Bolt platform under this agreement.
* *Note*: Data protection law does not prevent this sharing, provided:
** the information is necessary for contract performance or legal compliance,
** Bolt limits the disclosure to only what is needed (e.g. "suspended due to a verified passenger safety complaint"), and
** the information is accurate and handled securely.

# *Column definitions*



# _fact_rides_order.count_regular_airport_yes_

On-demand rides booked right when needed

Rides booked in advance (scheduled ride feature)

# To what extent is July 2025 representative for an average month, or should we treat it as a peak period? Maybe we can look at a non-traditional holiday month? Or even better, a 12m period?

The figures in the Quick Calc tab account for seasonal trends by applying an internally approved Seasonality Adjustment (as seen in the 'annual trip adjusted for seasonality' metric).

# Are “regular” and “scheduled” rides fully distinct, or can a ride appear in both categories?

A ride is categorised based on its booking method - either on-demand ("regular") or in advance ("scheduled"). A single trip can only fall into one of these categories.

# To what extent is there some double counting related to airport drop off & airport pickup (e.g. same travel)

A ride _to_ the airport (drop-off) and a subsequent ride _from_ the airport (pickup) are correctly treated as two separate and distinct trips.

Hi [~accountid:5d8df399c7d4e30dc2836580] and [~accountid:620e4df5a713ab0068139e4a] please find below our legal assessment: 

*1. Worker Status Risk*
Asking drivers to go into the terminal, wait for passengers with name signs, help with bags, and follow specific service expectations may be seen as Bolt having more control over them. In legal terms, this increases the risk they could be classified as _workers_ rather than independent contractors.

*What we recommend:*

* Make the service completely optional for drivers – no penalties if they don’t take part.
* Present service instructions as guidelines, not mandatory rules.
* Clearly explain in any driver communications that they are free to decide how they greet passengers.

This won’t remove the risk entirely, but it shows we’re treating drivers as self-employed and helps protect our position if challenged.

2. *Licensing and Airport permissions* - we suggest getting approval from Public Policy team and that no further approvals are needed from the airport and TFL

3. *Data Privacy*
This pilot involves sharing more detailed passenger info with drivers (name, flight, terminal). If not handled carefully, this could raise GDPR issues.

*What we recommend:*

* Only pass on the information drivers really need (e.g. name and terminal – not full flight history).
* Confirm our privacy notices (especially for business clients) cover this type of data use.
* Remind drivers they must not misuse or store passenger details.

Adding here [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a] to confirm the above and provide his input. 

*4. Accessibility and Equality Risk*

If we present _Meet & Greet_ as a service for passengers with disabilities, then Bolt may take on legal duties under the Equality Act 2010, even if that wasn’t the original intention.

These legal duties could include:

* Ensuring the service is consistently available to disabled passengers,  not just when convenient;
* Ensuring drivers are trained to assist people with mobility, hearing, vision or cognitive issues;
* Possibly being required to provide the service at no extra cost, if it’s seen as a "reasonable adjustment" for accessibility.

If we don’t meet those expectations, we could face legal complaints or criticism for discrimination.

*What we recommend instead:*

* Describing it as a premium or convenience service - something for business travellers or anyone who wants a smoother airport pick-up.
* Avoid saying or implying that this is _specifically for people who have difficulty walking, navigating, or who have disabilities_.
* If asked, we can say it’s “open to any passenger who would prefer to be met inside the terminal.”

# *Fare Transparency*
The fare includes:

* A £14.50 parking fee
* A £20 cancellation fee

These must be clearly explained to customers to avoid complaints or claims under consumer law.

*What we recommend:*

* Make sure these fees are clearly shown when the ride is booked – including on Ride Booker and in confirmation emails.
* Review any cancellation messages to make sure they explain the £20 charge up front.

Hope this helps. Let me know if you have any questions.

Hey [~accountid:712020:bad8b035-3802-4b02-965b-cc2dd648c932] , thanks for raising this!

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
*TL;DR*
{panel}

*Low risk:*

* Collecting optional email addresses for follow-up is low-risk and expected by users
* Main privacy consideration is transparency and appropriate access controls
* Risk is easy to mitigate with small UI and process adjustments

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Summary of feature*
{panel}

* Riders at Schiphol can scan a QR code in the vehicle to access a short feedback form
* Feedback is anonymous by default, with an optional email field for follow-up
* All responses go to a Bolt employee for triage; serious issues get escalated to the fleet’s operational manager
* Survey is hosted on Typeform

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*Key privacy observations*
{panel}

* Optional email is fine and fits user expectations, but needs a short line explaining why we ask for it (see below)
* Since data may be shared with an operational manager, there’s a risk of over-disclosure if the rider includes identifiable or sensitive info in free text (e.g. "driver was aggressive toward me as a woman")
* Even if anonymous, feedback can contain implied identifiers (e.g. time/location of trip)
* Good that this avoids tying data back to ride records, this keeps risk low

❓ *Clarifying questions:*

* Will we use the feedback for anything beyond individual complaint handling (e.g. reporting, performance tracking)?
* Is the feedback shown as-is to operational managers, or do we plan to summarize/filter it?
* If, say, a rider gives anonymous feedback, but we’ll see that it’s a serious violation, will we cross-reference it to the trip that was active when the feedback was given and take action against the driver OR try and find who the rider was?

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Minimal changes to reduce risk*
{panel}

* Add a short note next to the email field: _“Optional - only if you’d like us to follow up”_
** This will be more transparent/reassuring the rider that they can skip the email field.
* Include a short privacy note (It might change based on your responses to my questions above):
** Your feedback helps us improve the experience at Schiphol. If you don’t share your email, your response will stay anonymous, please avoid including any personal data. If you choose to provide your email, we may contact you, and your personal data will be handled in line with our Privacy Notice for Passengers: [https://bolt.eu/nl-nl/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/nl-nl/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|smart-link] .  
* Please make sure that access to responses is given only to people who need to see it, and not, for example, to everyone/all employees.

In my eyes this Court ruling ([https://www.gesetze-rechtsprechung.sh.juris.de/jportal/recherche3doc/Schleswig-Holsteinisches_Oberlandesgericht_16_U_137-19_NJRE001436838.pdf?json={"format"%3A"pdf"%2C"docId"%3A"NJRE001436838"%2C"portalId"%3A"bssh"}&_=%2FSchleswig-Holsteinisches_Oberlandesgericht_16_U_137-19_NJRE001436838.pdf|https://www.gesetze-rechtsprechung.sh.juris.de/jportal/recherche3doc/Schleswig-Holsteinisches_Oberlandesgericht_16_U_137-19_NJRE001436838.pdf?json=%7B%22format%22%3A%22pdf%22%2C%22docId%22%3A%22NJRE001436838%22%2C%22portalId%22%3A%22bssh%22%7D&_=%2FSchleswig-Holsteinisches_Oberlandesgericht_16_U_137-19_NJRE001436838.pdf]) does not specify that anyone needs to provide third party data to anyone specifically. I merely says the following:

* Companies could have duties of cooperation and transparency (§ 242) _within each contract_, e.g. providing relevant data to the contracting party when legally entitled or necessary to exercise their rights (for instance, when a rider disputes a charge or a driver contests a suspension).

What the ruling did not say:
That Companies would have any direct duty (and in fact potentially a legal prohibition) to share personal or transactional data of other customers (third party). This would potentially still violate data protection law as the court ruling does not overrule the GDPR.


I think that the case showcases something more abstract:

A company may need to disclose information that affects the legitimate interests of its _own contracting partner (the requesting party)_ when that partner explicitly asks for it and the purpose is legitimate but not information about _others_.

Hi team


In the UK we have Bolt Assist to support passengers with mobility impairments or who would like a little more guidance when travelling independently. We developed a series of videos / guidance for drivers to complete in order to be able to join the category. The videos can be viewed [here|https://bolt.eu/en-gb/driver/guide/accessibility-category-guidance/] and were developed in collaboration with Disability Rights UK. Drivers have to complete this guidance to then be able to offer trips on the Bolt Assist category which is designed specifically for older and disabled passengers. It includes information on the Equality Act, inclusive language, and how to offer additional assistance. I believe this guidance was shared with the CS team when the category launched for further information on how to support disabled passengers if they were to make a complaint to Bolt. Do let me know if not and I will speak with ops.

[~accountid:712020:8af2b159-71c0-448a-80ba-ff5059bb02f6] recently delivered a programme of consultation with a number of NGOs to inform our global processes on supporting vulnerable passengers experiencing safety incidents. This included how best to support disabled passengers and those who had been victims of sexual assault and harassment. As part of this I believe the team is now delivering a ‘Train the Trainer’ programme with Good Night Out, a UK based NGO who supports organisations operating in the Night Time Economy and the services that support their clients and staff. Egalita would you be able to provide an update on your programme of work as I think it’s super relevant here. 

For micromobility, we have developed tools to allow for cash payments to access our services. I think this aligns with the guidance from the FCA on how to ensure we are accounting for different groups. We also have offers such as Bolt for All, which offers discounted rides to low-income households. We also partner with NGOs including Sight Loss Councils to better understand the impact of micromobility services on people with sight loss. 

We have also signed the Women’s Night Safety Charter in London and in Manchester, and have made applications to sign the Night Safety Charter in the West Midlands. I think these are all good examples of how we are considering different customers within our services. 

I have asked for access to that document you shared [~accountid:712020:238a1b89-0f1b-4797-9066-90af4142a510] but let me know if you need any more information on this. 

Georgia

Some preliminary thoughts:

* Why do we need to agree anything directly with GE to begin with? Our arrangement is with TB as our customer. And if any limitation needs to be lifted or changes made per specific TB’s customer (GE) we should rather do it in the agreement with TB. _I know Tom has been looking into setups where person X leverages on person Y’s API integration while also having a direct arrangement with us (the likes of Sabre, Amadeus) but this is parked and there’s no clarity on how such setup would work._ 
* On the specific point of us allowing GE to add a margin to the ride price we might have room to commit to smth in the following lines: _“The Customer is_ +_not permitted_+ _to apply any fees or markups towards Passengers or other third parties in relation to rides requested through Ride Booker API_ +_in breach of the applicable laws_+_.”_ Meaning it’s fine as long as they ensure it’s done compliantly.
* What is the following part about though - “and we'll then send them this margin on a monthly basis”? Why should we be sending anything to them in relation to the margin they're collecting on their end? An why a rebate from us to GE on top?
* Let’s be super mindful about any third party “onselling/reselling rides” - it can be deemed a licensed (dispatch) activity if addressed to general public. A license which I doubt an average currency exchange retailer has. Under the current agreements we’re limiting these use cases precisely by prohibiting customer-imposed markups. Going forward we’d rather go with something in the below lines as the default. What geo’s are we talking about here?

_The Company may use its access to Ride Booker API to request Ride-Hailing Services to persons that are entitled to benefit from such service due to their existing client or similar relationship with the Company whereas the_ +_Company may not use Ride Booker for intermediating Ride-Hailing Services to the public_+ _or for providing dispatcher or similar services or for submission of Ride Requests_ +_in breach of the applicable laws_+_._

* Overall, it reminds me of the kiosk use case where it’s actually Bolt who should be owning the consumer relation but we’re trying to hack it with RB API which is designed for the likes of TB (b2b) to own the subsequent relationship with the consumer (b2b2c). Though I understand with kiosks for the pilot phase the business is accepting the possible backlash from empowering our API customers doing smth which might not be compliant.

Apologize for having more questions than answers at this point.
